[article] Neural Message Passing for Quantum Chemistry
[claim] The Message Passing Neural Network (MPNN) achieves state‑of‑the‑art performance on all QM9 regression targets, reaching chemical accuracy on 11 of the 13 targets and outperforming prior models such as SchNet and DTNN.
[claim] Inference with the MPNN takes roughly 10⁻² seconds per molecule, about 300,000 times faster than the DFT reference calculation (~10³ seconds).
[claim] The multiple‑tower architecture reduces the computational complexity of a propagation step from O(n²d²) to O(n²d²/k) and yields a 2× speedup for n=9, d=200, k=8.
[claim] A general training method allows MPNNs to use larger node representation dimensions without increasing computation time or memory, providing substantial savings over previous high‑dimensional MPNNs.
[claim] Introducing a virtual edge type for pairs of non‑connected nodes enables long‑distance information propagation during message passing.
[claim] Adding a latent master node that connects to every atom provides a global scratch space, allowing larger hidden dimensions with minimal performance penalty.
[claim] Using a pair‑message function that depends on both source and destination node states improves message‑passing efficiency compared with the standard matrix‑multiplication message function.
[claim] The Message Passing Neural Network framework unifies eight previously proposed graph‑based neural models under a single formalism.
[claim] Learning directly from molecular graphs without handcrafted descriptors enables the MPNN to achieve lower prediction errors than descriptor‑based methods.
[claim] Across all QM9 properties, the MPNN reduces the mean absolute error by 30–70 % relative to the best previously reported graph‑neural‑network baseline.
[claim] For internal energy at 0 K (U0), enthalpy (H), Gibbs free energy (G), heat capacity at constant volume (Cv), and highest vibrational frequency (Ω), the MPNN records lower mean absolute errors than SchNet and DTNN (U0 MAE 0.45 vs 0.55/0.72; H 0.39 vs 0.59/0.80; G 0.44 vs 0.55/0.74; Cv 0.80 vs 0.99/1.71; Ω 0.19 vs 0.41/0.78).
[future_topic] datasets with larger molecules

[article] SchNet: A continuous-filter convolutional neural network for modeling quantum interactions
[claim] Continuous-filter convolutional (cfconv) layers enable convolution on arbitrarily positioned inputs, overcoming the limitations of discrete filters that require grid-aligned data.
[claim] SchNet provides rotationally invariant energy predictions and rotationally equivariant, energy‑conserving force predictions by defining forces as the negative gradient of the predicted energy.
[claim] When trained on MD17 trajectories with a combined energy‑and‑force loss, SchNet achieves energy MAE ≤0.12 kcal/mol and force MAE ≤0.33 kcal/mol/Å, matching or surpassing GDML and DTNN on all tested molecules, including flexible ones such as malonaldehyde and ethanol.
[claim] Training SchNet with forces on only 1,000 examples yields better accuracy than training on 50,000 examples using energies alone, demonstrating that force information improves data efficiency.
[claim] On the ISO17 benchmark, SchNet reaches chemical‑accuracy (≈0.5 kcal/mol MAE) for energy predictions on molecules seen during training and further improves predictions on unseen isomers when forces are included in training.
[claim] Including force information in the training loss causally improves SchNet’s generalization to previously unseen chemical structures in ISO17.
[claim] GDML cannot be trained on 50,000 MD17 examples due to its quadratic scaling with the number of atoms and samples, whereas SchNet scales to that dataset size.
[claim] The ISO17 benchmark, comprising 645,000 conformations of 129 C7O2H10 isomers, is introduced to evaluate models on combined chemical and conformational variation.
[claim] Using a shifted softplus activation guarantees an infinitely differentiable (smooth) potential energy surface, facilitating geometry optimization.
[claim] Continuous-filter convolutions produce smoother energy predictions than discrete filters, as illustrated in Figure 1.
[claim] On the QM9 benchmark, SchNet attains a mean absolute error of 0.31 kcal/mol for total‑energy prediction with 110 k training examples, outperforming DTNN (0.84) and enn‑s2s (0.45).
[future_topic] more challenging benchmark with chemical and structural variations

[article] Artificial Intelligence for Multiscale Modeling in Solid-State Physics and Chemistry: A Comprehensive Review
[claim] Artificial intelligence has transformed multiscale modeling by linking atomic, mesoscale, and continuum scales, delivering improved accuracy and reduced computational cost compared with traditional methods.
[claim] Machine‑learning‑driven interatomic potentials (e.g., GAP, DeePMD) and DFT‑trained surrogate models enable simulations of up to millions of atoms while retaining accuracy close to first‑principles benchmarks, making large‑scale high‑fidelity simulations feasible.
[claim] Neural‑network‑based electronic‑structure prediction tools achieve significant speedups over conventional density‑functional theory while maintaining comparable accuracy, accelerating electronic‑structure calculations.
[claim] Graph neural network architectures such as MEGNet and SchNet enhance prediction of phase transitions, defect dynamics, and bulk material properties relative to classical computational approaches.
[claim] The multiscale structural complexity measure introduced by Bagrov et al. detects phase transitions in classical spin systems via a sharp extremum in the temperature derivative dC/dT.
[claim] Integrating renormalization‑group concepts with machine‑learning architectures has been used to predict transitions to canted antiferromagnetic phases in 3D Ising and Fermi‑Hubbard models, to classify quantum phases, and to recognize complex many‑body phases from raw simulation data.
[claim] Current challenges limiting AI‑driven multiscale modeling include limited data availability, restricted model transferability, and limited explainability.
[claim] Future integration of formal renormalization‑group concepts with machine‑learning architectures is a promising direction for modeling systems near criticality or with strong electron correlations.
[future_topic] Machine learning force fields
[future_topic] Graph neural networks
[future_topic] AI-accelerated electronic structure prediction
[future_topic] Data-driven multiscale modeling

[article] MACE: Higher Order Equivariant Message Passing Neural Networks for Fast and Accurate Force Fields
[claim] MACE uses four-body (higher-order) messages, allowing only two message‑passing layers to achieve converged accuracy, whereas prior equivariant MPNNs required five or six layers.
[claim] MACE attains state‑of‑the‑art accuracy, achieving lower root‑mean‑square energy and force errors than previous models on the rMD17, 3BPA, and AcAc benchmark suites.
[claim] MACE evaluates roughly ten times faster than prior force‑field models for invariant (L=0) architectures and 4–5 times faster for equivariant (L=1,2) architectures, while delivering lower prediction errors.
[claim] MACE shows superior extrapolation ability, reducing energy RMSE by about 30 % at 1200 K and 40 % on dihedral‑slice energies for the 3BPA benchmark, and achieving lower errors on geometries far from the training distribution.
[claim] On the 3BPA molecule energy profile, MACE predictions are closest to the DFT ground truth across three dihedral slices, outperforming BOTNet and NequIP.
[claim] MACE reaches high accuracy rapidly, matching a converged BOTNet model on the 3BPA dataset after roughly 30 minutes of training on an NVIDIA A100 GPU, and trains each benchmark dataset in 2–6 hours.
[claim] The computational cost of MACE scales O(1) with the number of chemical elements because species embeddings are continuous and not included in the tensor‑product contraction, and higher‑order features are implemented via an efficient single‑loop tensor‑contraction algorithm.
[claim] By decoupling body‑order from the number of message‑passing iterations, MACE has a small receptive field of approximately 4–5 Å per layer, enabling efficient parallelisation across GPUs.
[claim] Increasing the correlation order of messages (ν) steepens the learning‑curve power law, yielding higher data efficiency.
[future_topic] Higher body order messages
[future_topic] Learning curve power‑law behavior
[future_topic] Extrapolation benchmark generalization

[article] General framework for E(3)-equivariant neural network representation of density functional theory Hamiltonian
[claim] DeepH-E3 provides a universal E(3)-equivariant deep-learning framework that exactly preserves Euclidean symmetry of the DFT Hamiltonian, including spin-orbit coupling.
[claim] DeepH-E3 predicts DFT Hamiltonian matrix elements with sub‑meV mean absolute error, reducing the error by roughly a factor of two compared with the original DeepH method across diverse material systems.
[claim] DeepH-E3 enables accurate electronic‑structure calculations for supercells larger than 10⁴ atoms, reducing computational cost by several orders of magnitude and allowing calculations in minutes on a single GPU versus months on thousands of CPU cores.
[claim] DeepH‑E3 reproduces the band structure of magic‑angle twisted bilayer graphene (θ = 1.08°, 11 164 atoms) in excellent agreement with DFT and low‑energy continuum models, correctly capturing the flat bands near the Fermi level.
[claim] DeepH‑E3 predicts a spin‑orbit‑coupling‑induced topological quantum phase transition in twisted bilayer Bi₂Te₃, evidenced by band‑gap closing and reopening and a change of the Z₂ invariant from 0 to 1 as SOC strength increases.
[claim] DeepH‑E3 attains sub‑meV accuracy after training on only a few hundred DFT calculations of small, non‑twisted structures, demonstrating high data efficiency.
[claim] DeepH‑E3 generalizes across diverse material systems—including graphene, MoS₂, bismuthene, Bi₂Se₃, and Bi₂Te₃—achieving consistently sub‑meV Hamiltonian prediction errors.
[claim] The model generalizes to arbitrarily twisted bilayer structures; the mean absolute error of Hamiltonian predictions decreases as the Moiré supercell size grows (or twist angle decreases).
[claim] The equivariant architecture handles spin‑orbital Hamiltonians by separating real and imaginary components and applying a change‑of‑basis for half‑integer representations, thereby preserving equivariance without requiring complex‑valued network layers.
[claim] The model can fit 2.8 × 10⁹ non‑zero complex‑valued Hamiltonian matrix elements with only ~10⁵ real trainable parameters, indicating high capacity efficiency.
[future_topic] Construction of a Moiré‑twisted material database using DeepH‑E3
[future_topic] Extension of E(3)‑equivariant neural networks to capture DeepH’s small‑to‑large scale learning capability

[article] Phonon predictions with E(3)-equivariant graph neural networks
[claim] Phonax efficiently predicts phonon dispersion relations and density of states for inorganic crystal materials.
[claim] Including Hessian (second‑derivative) data in training improves the energy model accuracy beyond training with only energy and force data, reduces force MAE, and provides an effective ~7× increase in the amount of force information.
[claim] Augmenting a minimal 1×1×1 supercell training set with Hessian data yields more accurate phonon predictions than training on a larger 3×3×3 supercell alone.
[claim] The E(3)-equivariant graph neural network architecture automatically preserves crystalline symmetries, yielding the correct acoustic‑sum‑rule zero modes without additional corrections.
[claim] Phonax can predict molecular vibrational spectra and correctly assign IR/Raman active modes by analyzing irreducible representations.
[claim] Fine‑tuning an energy model on a benzene vibrational spectrum improves spectrum predictions for unseen molecules such as toluene and phenol.
[claim] A generalized energy model that includes external electric‑field dependence can predict polarization, Born effective charges, and polarizability, and improves energy and force MAE.
[claim] The Phonax framework works for both periodic crystals and isolated molecules and can be extended to higher‑order derivatives such as field‑dependent properties.
[future_topic] Generalized energy models that include external fields
[future_topic] High‑throughput AI‑guided material design frameworks incorporating phonon predictions
[future_topic] Application of equivariant GNN phonon predictions to drug‑discovery related molecular systems
[future_topic] Extension of Hessian‑based training to other higher‑order physical observables

[article] GNN-Assisted Phase Space Integration with Application to Atomistics
[claim] Standard Gaussian quadrature rules produce frame‑dependent (non‑objective) phase‑averaged internal energies for rotated crystal lattices.
[claim] Gaussian quadrature leads to abrupt energy jumps and fictitious minima when neighbor cut‑off radii change during large deformations.
[claim] Third‑order Gaussian quadrature fails to approximate phase‑space integrals for bulk aluminum above 300 K, producing spurious minima in the Helmholtz free‑energy landscape.
[claim] Fifth‑order Gaussian quadrature yields internal energies and free‑energy curves that remain in good agreement with molecular dynamics results across the full temperature range studied.
[claim] An E(3)‑equivariant graph neural network architecture guarantees rotational invariance of predicted phase‑averaged quantities.
[claim] The E(3)‑equivariant GNN surrogate provides superior accuracy compared with third‑ and fifth‑order Gaussian quadrature for thermal expansion of copper, martensitic phase transition of iron, and grain‑boundary energy calculations, matching molecular dynamics reference data.
[claim] The GNN surrogate achieves mean absolute errors of ≤0.313 meV for energy, ≤0.189 meV/Å for forces, and ≤0.0734 meV/Å² for thermal forces on validation sets.
[claim] Inference with the trained GNN is significantly faster than evaluating fifth‑order Gaussian quadrature, enabling frequent high‑dimensional integral evaluations and quasistatic finite‑temperature atomistic simulations without costly MD averaging.
[claim] Training the GNN on high‑fidelity Monte‑Carlo integration data enables accurate prediction of phase‑averaged energies and their derivatives for atomic clusters.
[claim] The GNN‑assisted integration framework can be applied to high‑dimensional integration problems beyond atomistics.
[claim] Incorporating E(3)‑equivariance into the GNN architecture provides a significant performance boost over standard multilayer perceptrons for phase‑space integration tasks.
[future_topic] Application of GNN‑assisted phase‑space integration to financial mathematics (e.g., pricing of derivatives)

[article] Predicting ionic conductivity in solids from the machine-learned potential energy landscape
[claim] The frozen-framework PES descriptor screening ranks lithium-containing Materials Project compounds such that eight of the ten highest‑ranked materials are confirmed to be room‑temperature superionic conductors by first‑principles calculations.
[claim] The proposed screening method is approximately 50 × faster than molecular dynamics driven by a machine‑learning interatomic potential and at least 3 000 × faster than first‑principles molecular dynamics.
[claim] The combined descriptor Ξ, defined as the product of sigmoid‑transformed connected and disconnected free‑volume descriptors at a 0.5 eV threshold, achieves higher ranking scores than each individual descriptor and far exceeds random‑guess performance.
[claim] Free‑volume (FV) descriptors evaluated at energy thresholds between 0.3 eV and 0.5 eV consistently outperform or match the minimal percolation energy (MPE) descriptor across all three evaluation scores.
[claim] Using the frozen‑framework approximation, where only a single Li ion moves while the host lattice remains fixed, reduces the generalization error of the ML‑IAP compared with fully relaxed MD or NEB simulations.
[claim] AIMD simulations of the five top‑Ξ candidates confirm high ionic conductivities (e.g., Li(BH)6 shows σ ≈ 0.9 S cm⁻¹ at 1000 K with activation energy 219 ± 86 meV), validating the screening predictions.
[claim] The screening pipeline, when applied to 5 997 lithium‑containing Materials Project structures that satisfy basic stability and band‑gap criteria, yields 1302 structures after removing transition‑metal containing compounds, of which 113 have Ξ > 0.25.
[claim] The proposed descriptor‑based screening approach is not tied to a specific ML‑IAP; it can be employed with any universal interatomic potential model.
[claim] All evaluated descriptors (MPE, FV‑connected, FV‑disconnected) achieve ranking scores above those of a random‑guess classifier, demonstrating predictive capability for ionic conductivity.
[claim] Finite‑size tests using a larger supercell and an ML‑IAP (SevenNet) show that diffusion coefficients converge within statistical uncertainties, confirming that the AIMD results are not significantly affected by supercell size.
[claim] The Ξ descriptor screening increases the proportion of room‑temperature superionic candidates from ~7% in an unbiased sample to 55% in the top‑100 Ξ‑ranked list, an ~8‑fold improvement.
[claim] AIMD simulations of the ten highest‑ranking Ξ‑predicted materials show that eight of them are superionic at room temperature.

[article] Machine Learning-Guided Discovery of Temperature-Induced Solid-Solid Phase Transitions in Inorganic Materials
[claim] A graph convolutional neural network predicts vibrational free energies with root‑mean‑square errors of 8.23 meV/atom (training), 11.34 meV/atom (validation) and 12.31 meV/atom (test), and its predictions for MgS and NaH polymorphs match DFT‑computed values across the 200–700 K range.
[claim] Screening of approximately 50 000 inorganic crystals with the machine‑learning model identified over 2 000 temperature‑induced solid‑solid polymorphic transitions between 300 K and 600 K, including 130 stable transitions within the technologically relevant 300 K–350 K interval.
[claim] Twenty‑one stable polar‑nonpolar transitions are predicted to exhibit relative lattice‑thermal‑conductivity changes of at least 20 % (0.20), ranging up to a 73 % increase for ZrSeO with a conductivity ratio of 1.73.
[claim] Several predicted solid‑solid transitions show large entropy changes exceeding 300 J K⁻¹ kg⁻¹ (e.g., Li₃MnF₇: 342.3 J K⁻¹ kg⁻¹, PnCl₂: 338.3 J K⁻¹ kg⁻¹, Fe₄OF₇: 252.1 J K⁻¹ kg⁻¹), while the highest entropy changes (> 400 J K⁻¹ kg⁻¹) are limited to transitions above 450 K and occur exclusively in nonpolar‑nonpolar categories, reducing their relevance for room‑temperature applications.
[claim] The presented workflow enables high‑throughput prediction of temperature‑induced solid‑solid phase transitions without performing explicit phonon calculations for each material, dramatically reducing computational cost.
[claim] Validation against experimental reports and independent first‑principles calculations confirms the robustness and predictive power of the ML‑guided framework, with reasonable agreement for transition temperatures of KNO₃, KNO₂ and CaCO₃, DFT‑calculated free‑energy differences matching ML predictions for a ten‑material subset, and thermal‑conductivity ratios for Li₄TiS₄ and NaNO₃ closely reproduced by DFT.
[claim] Uncertainty quantification based on latent‑space Euclidean distance provides error estimates that correlate with prediction errors, allowing exclusion of transitions whose uncertainty exceeds 50 % of the absolute free‑energy difference.
[claim] Polar‑nonpolar and polar‑polar transitions are more numerous than nonpolar‑nonpolar ones, with 214 polar‑nonpolar, 173 polar‑polar and 228 nonpolar‑nonpolar stable transitions predicted in the 300 K–600 K range.
[claim] Metastable phase transitions outnumber stable transitions across all symmetry categories in the screened dataset.
[claim] Across the screened temperature range, a larger number of predicted stable phase transitions is generally associated with smaller phase‑transition entropy changes.
[claim] The current screening neglects thermal‑expansion effects, which may cause discrepancies with experimental transition temperatures, especially when expansion strongly influences phase stability.
[future_topic] generative models

[article] Bridging scales with Machine Learning: From first principles statistical mechanics to continuum phase field computations to study order-disorder transitions in LixCoO2
[claim] A Hubbard U parameter of 2.5 eV in DFT+U (with a vdW‑DF exchange‑correlation functional) reproduces the experimental average lithiation voltages of LiCoO₂ across the composition ranges {0‑1}, {0‑0.5}, and {0.5‑1}.
[claim] A cluster expansion fitted to 333 DFT‑computed LiCoO₂ configurations using a genetic‑algorithm‑guided sparse regression achieves a root‑mean‑square error of 2.49 meV per primitive cell under 10‑fold cross‑validation and accurately reproduces formation energies, especially for configurations on or near the convex hull.
[claim] Large‑scale DFT calculations estimate the coherent anti‑phase boundary energy between the η₁ = ½ and η₃ = ½ ordered LiCoO₂ rotational variants to be 30.9 mJ m⁻².
[claim] Integrable Deep Neural Networks trained on derivative (chemical‑potential) data accurately learn the high‑dimensional free‑energy density and chemical‑potential functions for LiₓCoO₂, achieving mean‑squared errors comparable to the reported minima and reproducing DFT formation energies with a mean absolute error below 5 meV atom⁻¹.
[claim] Using the IDNN reduces the computational cost of generating free‑energy data for continuum models by approximately two orders of magnitude compared with direct DFT sampling.
[claim] Phase‑field simulations using the IDNN‑derived free‑energy density predict nucleation rates of the ordered phase at 260 K that are an order of magnitude higher than at 300 K, consistent with a larger free‑energy decrease (1 meV vs 0.5 meV per unit cell).
[claim] The presented scale‑bridging framework, linking DFT‑informed statistical mechanics to continuum phase‑field models via IDNN‑learned free‑energy functions, constitutes the first systematic implementation of this kind for LiCoO₂ cathodes.
[claim] Semi‑Grand Canonical Monte Carlo simulations predict an order‑disorder transition temperature slightly above 330 K for the x≈0.5 zig‑zag ordering, in agreement with experimental observations.
[claim] Monte Carlo simulations predict an additional ordered phase at Li composition x ≈ 1/3 that becomes stable below roughly 235 K, a phenomenon not observed at room temperature but reported in low‑temperature experiments.
[claim] Inclusion of van der Waals interactions together with DFT+U improves the accuracy of predicted order‑disorder transition temperatures for LiCoO₂ relative to earlier first‑principles studies.
[claim] Assuming the order‑disorder interface energy is half the anti‑phase boundary energy, the interface energy employed in phase‑field simulations is approximately 15.45 mJ m⁻².
[claim] Monte Carlo‑derived voltage profiles at 300 K match experimental measurements except that the metal‑insulator transition plateau near x≈0.8‑0.9 is not captured because the O3 structure was used.

[article] Matbench Discovery: A framework to evaluate machine learning crystal stability predictions
[claim] EquiformerV2+DeNS (a universal interatomic potential) achieves the highest classification performance among all evaluated models, with F1 scores up to 0.983, ROC AUC 0.96, and discovery acceleration factors up to 6.33, establishing state‑of‑the‑art for ML‑guided materials discovery.
[claim] Training universal interatomic potential models with forces, stresses, and magnetic moments substantially improves stability‑prediction performance compared with energy‑only models, enhancing both classification metrics (F1, DAF) and regression metrics (MAE, RMSE).
[claim] Regression‑based metrics such as MAE, RMSE, and R² are poorly aligned with classification‑based metrics needed for materials‑discovery tasks, and improvements in these regression metrics do not necessarily translate into higher F1 or discovery acceleration scores.
[claim] The WBM test set contains 215,488 unique prototype structures (32,942 thermodynamically stable), is enriched in actinides, lanthanides, metalloids and noble‑transition metals while under‑representing oxygen, is dominated by ternary phases (~75 %), and most structures have fewer than 100 atomic sites, contrasting with the Materials Project training distribution.
[claim] Prospective benchmarking that introduces covariate shift between training and test distributions provides a more realistic indicator of real‑world discovery performance than retrospective split strategies, and requires training and test sets larger than the training set to evaluate model scalability.
[claim] Random‑forest models excel on small datasets but are outperformed by neural‑network models on large datasets due to the benefits of representation learning.
[claim] Optimizing hyperparameters solely for the Matbench Discovery benchmark may degrade performance of models intended for general‑purpose use.
[claim] Models trained on Materials Project data systematically underpredict convex‑hull distances because the training set is biased toward low‑formation‑energy (stable) structures.
[claim] High disagreement among model predictions (large standard deviation) can be used to flag potential DFT relaxation failures in high‑throughput screenings.
[claim] Accurate regression models can still produce high false‑positive rates near the 0 eV/atom convex‑hull decision boundary.
[claim] Using the MACE checkpoint trained on the M3GNet dataset caused volume implosion failures for several hundred of the 250 k test crystals, whereas the checkpoint trained on the MPtrj dataset reduced failures to only 44 crystals.
[claim] Extrapolation performance degrades with increasing WBM batch number for most models, especially Wrenformer and Voronoi RF, while universal interatomic potential models (e.g., EquiformerV2, ORB) show minimal degradation across batches.

[article] E(3)-Equivariant Graph Neural Networks for Data-Efficient and Accurate Interatomic Potentials
[claim] NequIP achieves state-of-the-art accuracy on the MD-17 benchmark, surpassing invariant GNN‑IPs, shallow neural networks, and kernel‑based methods.
[claim] NequIP outperforms kernel‑based approaches such as sGDML and FCHL19/GPR across benchmarks, including small-data regimes and the MD-17 dataset.
[claim] NequIP requires up to three orders of magnitude fewer training configurations than existing neural interatomic potentials to reach comparable accuracy.
[claim] When trained on only 133 structures (~1 k frames), NequIP outperforms DeepMD trained on 133,500 structures for liquid water and ice simulations.
[claim] Using higher-order E(3)-equivariant representations (increasing rotation order from l=0 to l=1 and up to l=3) consistently reduces prediction error and improves accuracy across all evaluated tasks.
[claim] Predicting forces as the negative gradient of the learned total energy guarantees energy conservation and rotation‑equivariant forces.
[claim] The equivariant architecture scales linearly with the number of atoms because convolutions are limited to a local cutoff radius.
[claim] NequIP attains chemical‑accuracy energy errors (~2 meV) on CCSD(T) benchmark molecules using only 1,000 reference configurations, outperforming sGDML and GemNet.
[claim] NequIP reproduces structural and kinetic properties from ab‑initio molecular dynamics simulations with high fidelity.
[future_topic] high-order quantum chemical level of theory as reference
[future_topic] high-fidelity molecular dynamics simulations over long time scales
[method] NequIP

[article] A SURVEY OF AI FOR MATERIALS SCIENCE: FOUNDATION MODELS, LLM AGENTS, DATASETS, AND TOOLS
[claim] Foundation models enable cross-domain generalization and emergent capabilities for scientific discovery in materials science.
[claim] GNoME discovered over 2.2 million new stable inorganic materials and more than 45 000 new crystal prototypes, an order‑of‑magnitude increase over prior discovery efforts.
[claim] MACE‑MP‑0 attains state‑of‑the‑art accuracy for periodic systems while preserving equivariant inductive biases.
[claim] Multimodal models such as nach0, MultiMat, and MatterChat demonstrate reasoning over combined structural, textual, and spectral data, whereas most current foundation models remain unimodal and lack integrated image, spectrum, and experimental‑metadata fusion.
[claim] Current foundation models in materials science suffer from limited generalizability, interpretability, data imbalance, safety concerns, inability to model long‑range interactions (electrostatics, dispersion, magnetism), and lack of synthesizability, phase‑stability, or safety constraints, restricting experimental feasibility of generated candidates.
[claim] The survey proposes a task‑driven taxonomy that organizes foundation models into six application areas: data extraction/interpretation/Q&A, atomistic simulation, property prediction, materials structure/design/discovery, process planning/discovery/optimization, and multiscale modeling.
[claim] LLM‑based agents such as HoneyComb, LLMatDesign, ChatMOF, MatAgent, and MatPilot have been developed to automate literature search, hypothesis generation, synthesis planning, and experimental verification in materials science.
[claim] Existing materials datasets are heavily skewed toward inorganic atomistic systems, with limited coverage of polymers, composites, and mesoscale phenomena, creating a critical data imbalance for foundation‑model training.
[claim] Future research should focus on scalable pretraining, continual learning, data governance, trustworthiness, and incorporation of physics‑informed constraints such as equivariance, quantum‑mechanical symmetries, and thermodynamic principles to improve accuracy, interpretability, and trustworthiness of foundation models.
[claim] The autonomous A‑Lab platform synthesized 41 of 58 targeted materials (71 % success) over a 17‑day experiment with minimal human intervention, demonstrating high‑throughput autonomous materials synthesis.
[claim] Benchmarks such as LLM4Mat‑Bench, MaCBench, and MatBench evaluate multiple models across millions of structures and dozens of properties, revealing significant performance differences and that domain‑specific pretraining yields substantial improvements on materials‑science tasks like property prediction and named‑entity recognition.
[claim] MatterSim, a zero‑shot machine‑learned interatomic potential trained on >17 million DFT‑labeled structures, supports universal simulation across all elements, temperatures and pressures, achieving energy prediction errors below 50 meV/atom even in high‑temperature, non‑equilibrium regimes.

[article] A Universal Graph Deep Learning Interatomic Potential for the Periodic Table
[claim] The final M3GNet interatomic potential achieves test mean absolute errors of 0.035 eV/atom for energy, 0.072 eV/Å for forces, and 0.41 GPa for stresses on a held‑out Materials Project dataset covering 89 elements.
[claim] Relaxing test crystals with M3GNet reduces median volume error from 2.4 % to 0.6 % and energy mean absolute error from 0.169 eV/atom to 0.035 eV/atom relative to DFT‑relaxed references.
[claim] A single‑CPU M3GNet relaxation completes in about 22 seconds, compared with 15 hours on 32 cores for DFT; pre‑relaxation with M3GNet shortens subsequent DFT relaxation time by roughly a factor of three and reduces total CPU time by an average factor of 2.97.
[claim] Screening 31.7 million hypothetical crystals with M3GNet identifies approximately 1.8 million candidates with predicted hull distances below 0.001 eV/atom, and among the 2,000 lowest‑energy candidates, 1,578 are confirmed stable (Ehull < 0.001 eV/atom) by DFT.
[claim] Training M3GNet on energies alone (M3GNet‑E) yields force and stress mean absolute errors larger than the intrinsic data dispersion, demonstrating that forces and stresses must be included in training.
[claim] A single universal M3GNet model trained simultaneously on six elements attains error metrics comparable to element‑specific M3GNet models.
[claim] M3GNet predicts phonon band structures and densities of states for SiO₂ polymorphs that quantitatively agree with DFT calculations, and the predicted phonon density‑of‑states center follows the expected ω ∝ 1/√m trend across materials.
[claim] M3GNet molecular‑dynamics simulations of Li₃YCl₆ reproduce ionic conductivity (14.3 mS cm⁻¹) and activation energy (0.22 eV) consistent with ab‑initio MD, and short‑time MD correctly identifies known lithium superionic conductors by their high mean‑squared displacements at elevated temperatures.
[claim] On the MD17 and MD17‑CCSD(T) molecular force‑field benchmarks, M3GNet achieves lower energy and force errors than the Embedded Atom Neural Network and comparable accuracy to state‑of‑the‑art message‑passing and equivariant neural networks; when benchmarked against quantum‑accurate CCSD/CCSD(T) data, it attains state‑of‑the‑art accuracy for several molecules.
[claim] Across nine MatBench structural property datasets, M3GNet yields lower mean absolute errors than MODNet, AtomSets‑V1, MEGNet, and AutoMatminer, with improvements of 20.5 %–41.3 % on large datasets such as perovskite formation energy and MP band gap, and demonstrates excellent prediction accuracy on the broader MatBench suite.
[claim] For a MgO test set, M3GNet outperforms Moment Tensor Potentials in extrapolating equation‑of‑state behavior beyond the training regime and exhibits long‑range interaction characteristics similar to a Buckingham + Coulomb model.
[claim] The M3GNet architecture preserves continuity of energies, forces, and stresses with respect to changes in bond count, satisfying a necessary physical constraint for interatomic potentials.

[article] CHGNet: Pretrained universal neural network potential for charge-informed atomistic modeling
[claim] CHGNet achieves state-of-the-art performance on the Matbench Discovery benchmark, outperforming eight other submitted models.
[claim] On the Materials Project Trajectory test set, CHGNet trained with magnetic moment labels attains mean absolute errors of 30 meV/atom for energy, 77 meV/Å for forces, 0.348 GPa for stress, and 0.032 µB for magnetic moments.
[claim] CHGNet molecular dynamics simulations of Li superionic conductors reproduce room‑temperature ionic conductivities and activation energies within the error bars of AIMD, correctly distinguishing faster from slower conductors.
[claim] CHGNet integrates magnetic moment labels as a proxy for atomic charge, enabling inference of atomic charges and accurate differentiation of oxidation states such as V³⁺/V⁴⁺ and Fe²⁺/Fe³⁺.
[claim] In charge‑informed molecular dynamics of Li₀.₅MnO₂ at 1100 K, CHGNet predicts the emergence of Mn²⁺ after ~0.8 ns, coinciding with a ~50 meV/oxygen reduction in potential energy and the formation of a spinel‑like phase, indicating a correlation between charge disproportionation and phase transformation.
[claim] Including electronic entropy via charge‑decorated cluster expansions, CHGNet reproduces the experimentally observed miscibility gap and eutectoid‑like transition in the LiₓFePO₄ phase diagram, whereas a non‑charge‑decorated model fails to capture these features.
[claim] CHGNet accurately predicts the dramatic increase in Li‑ion diffusivity and the reduction of activation energy (~160 meV) in slightly Li‑stuffed Li₃La₃Te₂O₁₂, matching DFT‑computed values and the activated diffusion network theory.

[claim] LiFlow qualitatively captures ion transport behavior in sodium‑based conductors despite being trained only on lithium‑containing materials.

[article] LEARNING INTER-ATOMIC POTENTIALS WITHOUT EXPLICIT EQUIVARIANCE

[claim] TransIP learns an embedding where input rotations act approximately as a shared orthogonal transformation across different molecules despite no explicit equivariance in the architecture.
[claim] Energy predictions show near-linear scaling with equivariance error, while force predictions exhibit two-regime behavior with disproportionate gains at higher data scales.

[article] Generalization of Long-Range Machine Learning Potentials in Complex Chemical Spaces
[claim] Long-range correction schemes in machine learning interatomic potentials are essential for achieving state-of-the-art accuracy, improving in-distribution performance, and enabling significant gains in transferability to unseen regions of chemical space.
[claim] Latent Ewald Summation cannot infer correct partial charges without reference charge labels and frequently predicts charges near zero or opposite in sign to reference values in challenging chemical environments such as MOFs.
[claim] CELLI-based models trained with reference charges consistently produce physically meaningful results and exhibit good performance across biased split benchmarks on MOF datasets.
[claim] Baseline versions of MACE and Allegro are degenerate with respect to total charge and cannot distinguish between molecules with different charge states without long-range corrections.
[claim] Biased train-test splitting strategies including cluster, maximal separation, size, and random splits enable rigorous benchmarking by explicitly testing model performance in significantly different regions of chemical space.
[claim] EFA enables modeling of long-range interactions without requiring explicit neighbor cutoffs and outperforms CELLI on most benchmarking subsplits when reference charges are unavailable.
[claim] MACE without long-range correction does not generalize well to out-of-distribution samples, while integration of long-range correction schemes has significant effects on both MACE and Allegro architectures.
[claim] Strictly local MLIP models overestimate short-range interactions to compensate for missing or incorrectly modeled long-range contributions.
[claim] Metal-organic frameworks present an ideal application for MLIPs because classical force fields lack required accuracy while DFT is too computationally expensive for large unit cells and long timescales.
[claim] Increasing the number of message passing steps can lead to overfitting and decreased performance compared to baseline models.
[claim] Total charge embeddings can recover much of CELLI's performance on some datasets but generalize poorly in size-based extrapolation and should be viewed as a potential extension rather than replacement for long-range methods.
[claim] The observed improvements from long-range corrections cannot be attributed to increased model capacity as all variants share identical hyperparameters and nearly identical parameter counts.

[article] Scalable Parallel Algorithm for Graph Neural Network Interatomic Potentials in Molecular Dynamics Simulations
[claim] SevenNet achieves over 80% parallel efficiency in weak-scaling scenarios on a 32-GPU cluster with SiO2 benchmarks.

[claim] Spatial decomposition is a valid parallelization strategy only if the energy can be decomposed into atomic energies, which is key for the linear scalability of GNN-IPs.
[claim] SevenNet-0 successfully generated amorphous Si3N4 structure with 112,000 atoms through melt-quench MD simulation, reproducing key structural features matching DFT reference data.
[claim] The melt-quench simulation with 112,000 atoms on 8 GPUs demonstrated 0.94 parallel efficiency compared to single-GPU baseline.
[claim] SevenNet-0 shows improvements in energy and force accuracies compared to M3GNet (35 meV/atom, 0.072 eV/Å).

[claim] SevenNet-0, trained solely on crystal structures, reproduced key structural features of amorphous Si3N4 including fourfold coordination for Si and threefold coordination for N atoms.

[article] Pushing the limits of unconstrained machine-learned interatomic potentials
[claim] Unconstrained machine-learned interatomic potentials (MLIPs) trained on large datasets achieve accuracies on par with state-of-the-art equivariant architectures while maintaining orders-of-magnitude lower computational cost than quantum-mechanical methods.

[claim] The PET architecture scales to 730M parameters (OMat-XL) while maintaining tractable memory usage and computational efficiency due to increased node representation size and unconstrained architecture.
[claim] Conservative PET-OAM models achieve state-of-the-art performance on phonon tasks in matbench-discovery and the best overall accuracy in predicting shear modulus among tested models.
[claim] Non-conservative models allow residual asymmetries to drive relaxation toward more stable close-packed structures, unlike equivariant models that remain trapped in symmetric but unstable configurations, though 70% (16%) of final configurations retain symmetry of initial structure with 0.01 Å threshold for conservative (non-conservative) models.
[claim] Elastic moduli predictions are very sensitive to the lack of energy conservation in MLIP models, and non-conservative models consistently perform worse on matbench-discovery downstream tasks despite achieving better training and validation accuracies.
[claim] Central finite differences can more than halve the error for non-equivariant models on phonon calculations by averaging out inconsistencies between symmetry-equivalent displacements, and O(3)-averaging increases symmetric structures to 77% with symprec 0.01 Å in the non-conservative case.
[claim] Accurate conservative, rotationally unconstrained models can be used safely for phonon calculations, though it is recommended to use looser convergence tolerances or enforce rotational averaging when performing free geometry optimizations with unconstrained models, especially with direct-force predictions.
[claim] DFT setting inconsistency between training and evaluation datasets significantly affects MLIP model performance comparisons, with PET-OMAD performing worse than PET-OAM and PET-MPtrj on Inorganic Materials due to differences in ab initio theory levels.

[article] Orb-v3: atomistic simulation at scale
[claim] Orb-v3 achieves near state-of-the-art performance across evaluations with at least 10x reduction in latency and 8x reduction in memory compared to alternative MLIPs.

[article] Open Materials 2024 (OMat24) Inorganic Materials Dataset and Models

[article] EQUIFORMERV2: IMPROVED EQUIVARIANT TRANSFORMER FOR SCALING TO HIGHER-DEGREE REPRESENTATIONS

[claim] Attention re-normalization improves energy MAE by 2.4% while force MAE remains approximately the same.
[claim] Separable S2 activation prevents large gradients by separating activation for degree 0 and degree > 0 vectors, whereas directly replacing gate activation with S2 activation causes training instability and non-convergence.

[article] Benchmarking Materials Property Prediction Methods: The Matbench Test Set and Automatminer Reference Algorithm

[article] DeePMD-kit v2: A software package for Deep Potential models

[article] Large-scale machine-learning-assisted exploration of the whole materials space
[claim] CGAT-2 network achieves a mean absolute test error of 21 meV/atom for distance to the convex hull, enabling prediction of thermodynamic stability from unrelaxed crystal structures.

[article] Challenges and opportunities for machine learning in multiscale computational modeling
[claim] Machine learning can serve as a surrogate for, accelerate, or augment traditional numerical methods in multiscale computational modeling.

[claim] Hierarchical multiscale modeling approaches require large amounts of memory and storage space to store precomputed quantities of interest.
[claim] Concurrent multiscale modeling approaches face formidable computation costs as the problem size increases.
[claim] Trained ML models are typically only effective for interpolating data points and may not be reliable when extrapolating beyond the known data range.
[claim] Most common ML techniques such as CNNs are limited to specific discretization settings and do not generalize well to settings that differ from training data discretization.
[claim] Neural operators can make predictions that are not affected by discretization settings while maintaining prediction accuracy.
[claim] Physics-informed machine learning and transfer learning can reduce the need for large datasets while maintaining prediction accuracy and performance of ML models.
[claim] Physics-naïve ML architectures often fail to capture underlying physical laws despite having relatively high prediction performance.
[claim] Meta-learning allows ML algorithms to quickly learn and adapt to new tasks by leveraging experience from solving similar tasks with relatively small datasets.
[claim] ML can accelerate the solution of inverse problems by providing direct design solutions without requiring traditional iterative optimization processes.
[claim] Koopman operator theory allows highly nonlinear dynamical systems to be represented in terms of an infinite-dimensional linear operator.

[article] Machine-learning based interatomic potential for amorphous carbon
[claim] The Gaussian approximation potential (GAP) enables atomistic simulations with close-to-DFT accuracy at computational costs many orders of magnitude lower than quantum-mechanical methods.
[claim] Combined two-body, three-body, and SOAP many-body descriptors are necessary for GAP to achieve the accuracy limit imposed by force locality and make physically meaningful predictions; models using only subsets of descriptors produce unphysical structures during molecular dynamics simulations.
[claim] GAP predicts diamond lattice parameter (3.539 Å) very close to DFT-LDA reference (3.532 Å), outperforming screened Tersoff potential (3.566 Å), with bulk modulus and elastic constants reasonably close to DFT reference values.
[claim] GAP radial and angular distribution functions for liquid and amorphous carbon closely match DFT reference results, including peak locations, extents, and overall curve shapes.
[claim] GAP recovers three- and four-membered rings that are key features of liquid and low-density amorphous carbon structures, which empirical potentials (Tersoff/Brenner) fail to predict.
[claim] GAP fully reproduces the stability ordering of ta-C surface energies compared to DFT calculations, with differences less than 0.01 J m−2 for the most stable surface.
[claim] GAP predictions for Young's modulus of amorphous carbon agree very well with experimental values at all relevant densities, while screened Tersoff potential captures the trend but significantly overestimates absolute values.
[claim] GAP sp3 concentration predictions are closer to DFT reference than empirical Brenner and Tersoff potentials, particularly at lower densities; empirical potentials underestimate sp3 concentration in tetrahedral amorphous carbon.
[claim] Empirical potentials (Tersoff/Brenner) cannot describe interlayer spacing in graphite due to short-range cutoff being less than c/2, provide poor description of carbon surfaces, and yield much lower surface energies than GAP and DFT for ta-C surfaces.
[claim] Diamond exhibits strong force locality with force deviations vanishing practically at rfix = 5.5 Å, while graphite is highly nonlocal with larger force deviations that do not decay as rapidly.
[claim] For amorphous carbon with 3.7 Å cutoff radius, the lowest achievable standard deviation of force components is approximately 1 eV/Å due to fundamental nonlocality limits, representing a maximum accuracy bound for any finite-range interatomic potential.
[claim] DFT-based methods are practically limited to systems of a few hundred atoms, making generation of 8,000-atom amorphous carbon structures impossible with DFT-MD even on state-of-the-art supercomputers.

[article] The AFLOW Standard for High-Throughput Materials Science Calculations
[claim] The AFLOW standard enables reproducible high-throughput DFT calculations through standardized parameter sets for k-point density, energy cut-offs, exchange-correlation functionals, pseudopotentials, DFT+U parameters, and convergence criteria.
[claim] The AFLOWLIB repository contains calculated properties of over 625,000 materials across Binary Alloy Project, Electronic Structure database, Heusler database, and Elements database.
[claim] AFLOW calculations follow a standardized sequential workflow: RELAX1 → RELAX2 → STATIC → BANDS for materials in the Elements, ICSD, and Heusler databases.
[claim] Default NKPPRA values for non-BANDS calculations vary by database: Binary Alloy uses 6000 for RELAX, Heusler uses 10000 for STATIC and 6000 for RELAX, and ICSD uses 10000 for STATIC and 8000 for RELAX.
[claim] The PBE functional combined with PAW potentials is the default exchange-correlation functional and potential combination for ICSD, Binary Alloy, and Heusler databases.
[claim] The applied plane-wave kinetic energy cut-off (Ecut) is the largest recommended value among all species in the calculation, increased by a factor of 1.4.
[claim] DFT+U corrections are applied to the entire ICSD database and certain Heusler database entries containing O, S, Se, and F elements, but not to the Binary Alloy database.
[claim] Specific Ueff parameters are defined for d-block elements (Table 4) and U, J parameters for f-block elements (Table 5) to correct self-interaction error in DFT+U calculations, with values ranging from 1.9 eV (In) to 7.5 eV (Zn).
[claim] The first RELAX calculation is performed in collinear spin-polarized fashion with initial magnetic moments set to 1.0 µB per atom, and spin polarization is turned off in subsequent calculations if magnetization is below 0.025 µB/atom.
[claim] Electronic convergence criteria are δEelec = 10⁻⁵ eV and ionic convergence criteria are δEion = 10⁻⁴ eV for Elements database entries, while all other databases use δEelec = 10⁻³ eV and δEion = 10⁻² eV.
[claim] Following the AFLOW standard enables materials science researchers to reproduce AFLOWLIB consortium results and make direct comparisons of properties between different materials for identifying trends and formulating design rules.
[claim] BANDS calculations use 128 k-points per segment for single element structures and 20 k-points for compounds along high-symmetry paths.

[article] Machine Learning Interatomic Potentials: A Review and Framework for Understanding MLIPs
[claim] FastCHGNet trains in 1.5 hours using 32 GPUs compared to 8.3 days on a single A100 GPU for the original CHGNet model.
[claim] MLIPs map atomic configurations to total energy and provide forces and stresses as analytical derivatives of the potential energy surface.
[claim] MLIPs use highly flexible functional forms (e.g., neural networks) while PBPs use highly constrained forms guided by physical intuition (e.g., Lennard-Jones).
[claim] Approximately 40% of the UK's academic HPC was spent on DFT calculations in a recent year, most of which was AIMD.
[claim] EquiformerV2-OMAT24 achieves the best performance on the MatBench leaderboard as of this writing.
[claim] Each cataloged DFT structure provides one energy and 3N forces (N = number of atoms) for training universal MLIPs.
[claim] Pre-trained targeted MLIPs for specific systems can be found on the NIST Interatomic Potentials Repository and OpenKIM.
[claim] CHGNet achieves test mean absolute errors of 29 meV/atom for energy, 70 meV/Angstrom for force, and 0.308 GPa for stress.
[claim] M3GNet achieves test mean absolute errors of 35 meV/atom for energy, 72 meV/Angstrom for force, and 0.41 GPa for stress.
[claim] CHGNet uniquely includes electronic effects of valences by explicitly embedding magnetic moments on the vector representation of each atom, enabling charge-informed atomistic simulations.
[claim] CHGNet achieved the lowest formation energy MAE at 81 meV/atom, while all other models had MAEs of 129 meV/atom or higher.
[claim] MACE-MP0 performed best for discovering new stable materials with classification F1 score of 0.67, followed by CHGNet (0.61) and M3GNet (0.57).

[article] Discovering Melting Temperature Prediction Models of Inorganic Solids by Combining Supervised and Unsupervised Learning
[claim] A curated dataset of 476 binary ionic compound melting temperatures spanning 0-4,000°C was compiled for machine learning model development.
[claim] The best one-step gradient-boosted tree regression model achieves 165±4 K MAE and 0.89 R² on the test set for melting temperature prediction.
[claim] A two-step approach combining unsupervised clustering with supervised regression achieves 156±4 K MAE and 0.92 R², outperforming direct one-step supervised learning.
[claim] Cluster 1 (198 compounds, mostly ionic halides and oxides) achieves 136±5 K MAE and 0.92 R², while Cluster 2 (222 compounds, mostly covalent carbides and nitrides) achieves 189±7 K MAE and 0.90 R².
[claim] Cohesive energy and elastic moduli (shear and bulk modulus) are the most important features for melting temperature prediction, as identified by both ensemble feature importance and SHAP analysis.
[claim] Models trained without elastic moduli features yield errors greater than 400 K, demonstrating that elastic features are necessary for accurate melting temperature predictions.
[claim] Very-high melting temperatures (>3150 K) appear only in Cluster 2, predominantly in metal carbides, reflecting the covalent bonding character of these materials.
[claim] Tree ensemble methods (gradient-boosted trees and random forest regression) substantially outperform linear models, which achieve MAE >240 K and RMSE >340 K, at least 100 K worse than non-linear approaches.
[claim] The two-step clustering approach provides interpretability by revealing different melting physics dominated by bonding types, with Cluster 1 governed by ionic bonding features and Cluster 2 by covalent bonding features.
[claim] VS-SISSO symbolic regression generates interpretable expressions for melting temperature that provide qualitative insight into the melting physics dominating within each cluster.
[claim] Cluster 2 melting temperatures can be accurately represented with symbolic models depending on only two features: squared cohesive energy and inverse square root of periodic groups or electronegativities.
[claim] Symbolic regression results corroborate that cohesive energy and elastic moduli are the most important features, consistent with feature importance and SHAP analysis from tree ensemble models.

[article] Scaling deep learning for materials discovery
[claim] GNoME discovered 2.2 million crystal structures stable with respect to the Materials Project, with 381,000 newly on the convex hull, representing an order-of-magnitude expansion from all previous discoveries.
[claim] 736 GNoME-discovered structures match experimentally validated ICSD structures, with 184 representing novel discoveries since the project began.
[claim] GNoME achieves hit rates above 80% for structural predictions and 33% for composition-only predictions, compared to 1% in previous work, with active learning improving from less than 6% and 3% respectively over six rounds.
[claim] Final GNoME models predict energies with a mean absolute error of 11 meV per atom on relaxed structures, improved from 21 meV per atom in the initial model trained on Materials Project data.
[claim] GNNs trained on large and diverse first-principles calculations increase the number of stable crystals by more than an order of magnitude, with scaling showing consistent power-law improvements in MLIP accuracy and generalization on out-of-distribution structural tasks.
[claim] Large-scale pretraining of MLIPs on GNoME dataset enables models with unprecedented zero-shot accuracy on downstream AIMD data, outperforming state-of-the-art NequIP models trained on hundreds of structures from the target distribution.
[claim] GNoME discovered crystals correspond to 45,500 novel prototypes, a 5.6x increase from the 8,000 in Materials Project.
[claim] GNoME discovers approximately 52,000 layered materials compared to approximately 1,000 in Materials Project, and finds 528 promising Li-ion conductors, a 25x increase compared to the original study.
[claim] GNoME enables efficient discovery of materials with 4+ unique elements, which have been difficult for previous discovery efforts.
[claim] More than 10⁹ candidate structures were generated over the course of active learning using symmetry-aware partial substitutions and random structure search, with 232,477 out of 381,000 stable structures (approximately 61%) attributed to the SAPS candidate generation procedure.
[claim] GNoME-driven molecular dynamics simulations on 623 materials with previously unseen compositions enable classification of unseen compositions as superionic conductors in comparison with AIMD.
[claim] Crystal structures, data, and software for analyzing stable crystals, phase diagrams, static GNN, and interatomic potentials will be made available at the Google DeepMind materials_discovery GitHub repository and via the Materials Project with permanent DOI link 10.17188/2009989.

[method] M3GNet
[claim] The final M3GNet interatomic potential achieves test mean absolute errors of 0.035 eV/atom for energy, 0.072 eV/Å for forces, and 0.41 GPa for stresses on a held‑out Materials Project dataset covering 89 elements.
[claim] Relaxing test crystals with M3GNet reduces median volume error from 2.4 % to 0.6 % and energy mean absolute error from 0.169 eV/atom to 0.035 eV/atom relative to DFT‑relaxed references.
[claim] A single‑CPU M3GNet relaxation completes in about 22 seconds, compared with 15 hours on 32 cores for DFT; pre‑relaxation with M3GNet shortens subsequent DFT relaxation time by roughly a factor of three and reduces total CPU time by an average factor of 2.97.
[claim] Screening 31.7 million hypothetical crystals with M3GNet identifies approximately 1.8 million candidates with predicted hull distances below 0.001 eV/atom, and among the 2,000 lowest‑energy candidates, 1,578 are confirmed stable (Ehull < 0.001 eV/atom) by DFT.
[claim] Training M3GNet on energies alone (M3GNet‑E) yields force and stress mean absolute errors larger than the intrinsic data dispersion, demonstrating that forces and stresses must be included in training.
[claim] A single universal M3GNet model trained simultaneously on six elements attains error metrics comparable to element‑specific M3GNet models.
[claim] M3GNet predicts phonon band structures and densities of states for SiO₂ polymorphs that quantitatively agree with DFT calculations, and the predicted phonon density‑of‑states center follows the expected ω ∝ 1/√m trend across materials.
[claim] M3GNet molecular‑dynamics simulations of Li₃YCl₆ reproduce ionic conductivity (14.3 mS cm⁻¹) and activation energy (0.22 eV) consistent with ab‑initio MD, and short‑time MD correctly identifies known lithium superionic conductors by their high mean‑squared displacements at elevated temperatures.
[claim] On the MD17 and MD17‑CCSD(T) molecular force‑field benchmarks, M3GNet achieves lower energy and force errors than the Embedded Atom Neural Network and comparable accuracy to state‑of‑the‑art message‑passing and equivariant neural networks; when benchmarked against quantum‑accurate CCSD/CCSD(T) data, it attains state‑of‑the‑art accuracy for several molecules.
[claim] Across nine MatBench structural property datasets, M3GNet yields lower mean absolute errors than MODNet, AtomSets‑V1, MEGNet, and AutoMatminer, with improvements of 20.5 %–41.3 % on large datasets such as perovskite formation energy and MP band gap, and demonstrates excellent prediction accuracy on the broader MatBench suite.
[claim] For a MgO test set, M3GNet outperforms Moment Tensor Potentials in extrapolating equation‑of‑state behavior beyond the training regime and exhibits long‑range interaction characteristics similar to a Buckingham + Coulomb model.
[claim] The M3GNet architecture preserves continuity of energies, forces, and stresses with respect to changes in bond count, satisfying a necessary physical constraint for interatomic potentials.

[method] SchNet
[claim] Continuous-filter convolutional (cfconv) layers enable convolution on arbitrarily positioned inputs, overcoming the limitations of discrete filters that require grid-aligned data.
[claim] SchNet provides rotationally invariant energy predictions and rotationally equivariant, energy‑conserving force predictions by defining forces as the negative gradient of the predicted energy.
[claim] When trained on MD17 trajectories with a combined energy‑and‑force loss, SchNet achieves energy MAE ≤0.12 kcal/mol and force MAE ≤0.33 kcal/mol/Å, matching or surpassing GDML and DTNN on all tested molecules, including flexible ones such as malonaldehyde and ethanol.
[claim] Training SchNet with forces on only 1,000 examples yields better accuracy than training on 50,000 examples using energies alone, demonstrating that force information improves data efficiency.
[claim] On the ISO17 benchmark, SchNet reaches chemical‑accuracy (≈0.5 kcal/mol MAE) for energy predictions on molecules seen during training and further improves predictions on unseen isomers when forces are included in training.
[claim] Including force information in the training loss causally improves SchNet’s generalization to previously unseen chemical structures in ISO17.
[claim] GDML cannot be trained on 50,000 MD17 examples due to its quadratic scaling with the number of atoms and samples, whereas SchNet scales to that dataset size.
[claim] The ISO17 benchmark, comprising 645,000 conformations of 129 C7O2H10 isomers, is introduced to evaluate models on combined chemical and conformational variation.
[claim] Using a shifted softplus activation guarantees an infinitely differentiable (smooth) potential energy surface, facilitating geometry optimization.
[claim] Continuous-filter convolutions produce smoother energy predictions than discrete filters, as illustrated in Figure 1.
[claim] On the QM9 benchmark, SchNet attains a mean absolute error of 0.31 kcal/mol for total‑energy prediction with 110 k training examples, outperforming DTNN (0.84) and enn‑s2s (0.45).

[method] NequIP
[claim] NequIP achieves state-of-the-art accuracy on the MD-17 benchmark, surpassing invariant GNN‑IPs, shallow neural networks, and kernel‑based methods.
[claim] NequIP outperforms kernel‑based approaches such as sGDML and FCHL19/GPR across benchmarks, including small-data regimes and the MD-17 dataset.
[claim] NequIP requires up to three orders of magnitude fewer training configurations than existing neural interatomic potentials to reach comparable accuracy.
[claim] When trained on only 133 structures (~1 k frames), NequIP outperforms DeepMD trained on 133,500 structures for liquid water and ice simulations.
[claim] Using higher-order E(3)-equivariant representations (increasing rotation order from l=0 to l=1 and up to l=3) consistently reduces prediction error and improves accuracy across all evaluated tasks.
[claim] Predicting forces as the negative gradient of the learned total energy guarantees energy conservation and rotation‑equivariant forces.
[claim] The equivariant architecture scales linearly with the number of atoms because convolutions are limited to a local cutoff radius.
[claim] NequIP attains chemical‑accuracy energy errors (~2 meV) on CCSD(T) benchmark molecules using only 1,000 reference configurations, outperforming sGDML and GemNet.
[claim] NequIP reproduces structural and kinetic properties from ab‑initio molecular dynamics simulations with high fidelity.

[claim] DeepH-E3 provides a universal E(3)-equivariant deep-learning framework that exactly preserves Euclidean symmetry of the DFT Hamiltonian, including spin-orbit coupling.
[claim] DeepH-E3 predicts DFT Hamiltonian matrix elements with sub‑meV mean absolute error, reducing the error by roughly a factor of two compared with the original DeepH method across diverse material systems.
[claim] DeepH-E3 enables accurate electronic‑structure calculations for supercells larger than 10⁴ atoms, reducing computational cost by several orders of magnitude and allowing calculations in minutes on a single GPU versus months on thousands of CPU cores.
[claim] DeepH‑E3 reproduces the band structure of magic‑angle twisted bilayer graphene (θ = 1.08°, 11 164 atoms) in excellent agreement with DFT and low‑energy continuum models, correctly capturing the flat bands near the Fermi level.
[claim] DeepH‑E3 predicts a spin‑orbit‑coupling‑induced topological quantum phase transition in twisted bilayer Bi₂Te₃, evidenced by band‑gap closing and reopening and a change of the Z₂ invariant from 0 to 1 as SOC strength increases.
[claim] DeepH‑E3 attains sub‑meV accuracy after training on only a few hundred DFT calculations of small, non‑twisted structures, demonstrating high data efficiency.
[claim] DeepH‑E3 generalizes across diverse material systems—including graphene, MoS₂, bismuthene, Bi₂Se₃, and Bi₂Te₃—achieving consistently sub‑meV Hamiltonian prediction errors.
[claim] The model generalizes to arbitrarily twisted bilayer structures; the mean absolute error of Hamiltonian predictions decreases as the Moiré supercell size grows (or twist angle decreases).
[claim] The equivariant architecture handles spin‑orbital Hamiltonians by separating real and imaginary components and applying a change‑of‑basis for half‑integer representations, thereby preserving equivariance without requiring complex‑valued network layers.
[claim] The model can fit 2.8 × 10⁹ non‑zero complex‑valued Hamiltonian matrix elements with only ~10⁵ real trainable parameters, indicating high capacity efficiency.

[claim] Standard Gaussian quadrature rules produce frame‑dependent (non‑objective) phase‑averaged internal energies for rotated crystal lattices.
[claim] Gaussian quadrature leads to abrupt energy jumps and fictitious minima when neighbor cut‑off radii change during large deformations.
[claim] Third‑order Gaussian quadrature fails to approximate phase‑space integrals for bulk aluminum above 300 K, producing spurious minima in the Helmholtz free‑energy landscape.
[claim] Fifth‑order Gaussian quadrature yields internal energies and free‑energy curves that remain in good agreement with molecular dynamics results across the full temperature range studied.
[claim] An E(3)‑equivariant graph neural network architecture guarantees rotational invariance of predicted phase‑averaged quantities.
[claim] The E(3)‑equivariant GNN surrogate provides superior accuracy compared with third‑ and fifth‑order Gaussian quadrature for thermal expansion of copper, martensitic phase transition of iron, and grain‑boundary energy calculations, matching molecular dynamics reference data.
[claim] The GNN surrogate achieves mean absolute errors of ≤0.313 meV for energy, ≤0.189 meV/Å for forces, and ≤0.0734 meV/Å² for thermal forces on validation sets.
[claim] Inference with the trained GNN is significantly faster than evaluating fifth‑order Gaussian quadrature, enabling frequent high‑dimensional integral evaluations and quasistatic finite‑temperature atomistic simulations without costly MD averaging.
[claim] Training the GNN on high‑fidelity Monte‑Carlo integration data enables accurate prediction of phase‑averaged energies and their derivatives for atomic clusters.
[claim] The GNN‑assisted integration framework can be applied to high‑dimensional integration problems beyond atomistics.
[claim] Incorporating E(3)‑equivariance into the GNN architecture provides a significant performance boost over standard multilayer perceptrons for phase‑space integration tasks.

[claim] The combined descriptor Ξ, defined as the product of sigmoid‑transformed connected and disconnected free‑volume descriptors at a 0.5 eV threshold, achieves higher ranking scores than each individual descriptor and far exceeds random‑guess performance.
[claim] Free‑volume (FV) descriptors evaluated at energy thresholds between 0.3 eV and 0.5 eV consistently outperform or match the minimal percolation energy (MPE) descriptor across all three evaluation scores.
[claim] Using the frozen‑framework approximation, where only a single Li ion moves while the host lattice remains fixed, reduces the generalization error of the ML‑IAP compared with fully relaxed MD or NEB simulations.
[claim] AIMD simulations of the five top‑Ξ candidates confirm high ionic conductivities (e.g., Li(BH)6 shows σ ≈ 0.9 S cm⁻¹ at 1000 K with activation energy 219 ± 86 meV), validating the screening predictions.
[claim] The screening pipeline, when applied to 5 997 lithium‑containing Materials Project structures that satisfy basic stability and band‑gap criteria, yields 1302 structures after removing transition‑metal containing compounds, of which 113 have Ξ > 0.25.
[claim] The proposed descriptor‑based screening approach is not tied to a specific ML‑IAP; it can be employed with any universal interatomic potential model.
[claim] All evaluated descriptors (MPE, FV‑connected, FV‑disconnected) achieve ranking scores above those of a random‑guess classifier, demonstrating predictive capability for ionic conductivity.
[claim] Finite‑size tests using a larger supercell and an ML‑IAP (SevenNet) show that diffusion coefficients converge within statistical uncertainties, confirming that the AIMD results are not significantly affected by supercell size.
[claim] The Ξ descriptor screening increases the proportion of room‑temperature superionic candidates from ~7% in an unbiased sample to 55% in the top‑100 Ξ‑ranked list, an ~8‑fold improvement.
[claim] AIMD simulations of the ten highest‑ranking Ξ‑predicted materials show that eight of them are superionic at room temperature.

[method] Uncertainty-aware graph convolutional neural network for vibrational free‑energy prediction
[claim] A graph convolutional neural network predicts vibrational free energies with root‑mean‑square errors of 8.23 meV/atom (training), 11.34 meV/atom (validation) and 12.31 meV/atom (test), and its predictions for MgS and NaH polymorphs match DFT‑computed values across the 200–700 K range.
[claim] Screening of approximately 50 000 inorganic crystals with the machine‑learning model identified over 2 000 temperature‑induced solid‑solid polymorphic transitions between 300 K and 600 K, including 130 stable transitions within the technologically relevant 300 K–350 K interval.
[claim] Twenty‑one stable polar‑nonpolar transitions are predicted to exhibit relative lattice‑thermal‑conductivity changes of at least 20 % (0.20), ranging up to a 73 % increase for ZrSeO with a conductivity ratio of 1.73.
[claim] Several predicted solid‑solid transitions show large entropy changes exceeding 300 J K⁻¹ kg⁻¹ (e.g., Li₃MnF₇: 342.3 J K⁻¹ kg⁻¹, PnCl₂: 338.3 J K⁻¹ kg⁻¹, Fe₄OF₇: 252.1 J K⁻¹ kg⁻¹), while the highest entropy changes (> 400 J K⁻¹ kg⁻¹) are limited to transitions above 450 K and occur exclusively in nonpolar‑nonpolar categories, reducing their relevance for room‑temperature applications.
[claim] The presented workflow enables high‑throughput prediction of temperature‑induced solid‑solid phase transitions without performing explicit phonon calculations for each material, dramatically reducing computational cost.
[claim] Validation against experimental reports and independent first‑principles calculations confirms the robustness and predictive power of the ML‑guided framework, with reasonable agreement for transition temperatures of KNO₃, KNO₂ and CaCO₃, DFT‑calculated free‑energy differences matching ML predictions for a ten‑material subset, and thermal‑conductivity ratios for Li₄TiS₄ and NaNO₃ closely reproduced by DFT.
[claim] Uncertainty quantification based on latent‑space Euclidean distance provides error estimates that correlate with prediction errors, allowing exclusion of transitions whose uncertainty exceeds 50 % of the absolute free‑energy difference.
[claim] Polar‑nonpolar and polar‑polar transitions are more numerous than nonpolar‑nonpolar ones, with 214 polar‑nonpolar, 173 polar‑polar and 228 nonpolar‑nonpolar stable transitions predicted in the 300 K–600 K range.
[claim] Metastable phase transitions outnumber stable transitions across all symmetry categories in the screened dataset.
[claim] Across the screened temperature range, a larger number of predicted stable phase transitions is generally associated with smaller phase‑transition entropy changes.
[claim] The current screening neglects thermal‑expansion effects, which may cause discrepancies with experimental transition temperatures, especially when expansion strongly influences phase stability.

[method] Integrable Deep Neural Network (IDNN) for learning high‑dimensional free‑energy density and chemical potential functions
[claim] A Hubbard U parameter of 2.5 eV in DFT+U (with a vdW‑DF exchange‑correlation functional) reproduces the experimental average lithiation voltages of LiCoO₂ across the composition ranges {0‑1}, {0‑0.5}, and {0.5‑1}.
[claim] A cluster expansion fitted to 333 DFT‑computed LiCoO₂ configurations using a genetic‑algorithm‑guided sparse regression achieves a root‑mean‑square error of 2.49 meV per primitive cell under 10‑fold cross‑validation and accurately reproduces formation energies, especially for configurations on or near the convex hull.
[claim] Large‑scale DFT calculations estimate the coherent anti‑phase boundary energy between the η₁ = ½ and η₃ = ½ ordered LiCoO₂ rotational variants to be 30.9 mJ m⁻².
[claim] Integrable Deep Neural Networks trained on derivative (chemical‑potential) data accurately learn the high‑dimensional free‑energy density and chemical‑potential functions for LiₓCoO₂, achieving mean‑squared errors comparable to the reported minima and reproducing DFT formation energies with a mean absolute error below 5 meV atom⁻¹.
[claim] Using the IDNN reduces the computational cost of generating free‑energy data for continuum models by approximately two orders of magnitude compared with direct DFT sampling.
[claim] Phase‑field simulations using the IDNN‑derived free‑energy density predict nucleation rates of the ordered phase at 260 K that are an order of magnitude higher than at 300 K, consistent with a larger free‑energy decrease (1 meV vs 0.5 meV per unit cell).
[claim] The presented scale‑bridging framework, linking DFT‑informed statistical mechanics to continuum phase‑field models via IDNN‑learned free‑energy functions, constitutes the first systematic implementation of this kind for LiCoO₂ cathodes.
[claim] Semi‑Grand Canonical Monte Carlo simulations predict an order‑disorder transition temperature slightly above 330 K for the x≈0.5 zig‑zag ordering, in agreement with experimental observations.
[claim] Monte Carlo simulations predict an additional ordered phase at Li composition x ≈ 1/3 that becomes stable below roughly 235 K, a phenomenon not observed at room temperature but reported in low‑temperature experiments.
[claim] Inclusion of van der Waals interactions together with DFT+U improves the accuracy of predicted order‑disorder transition temperatures for LiCoO₂ relative to earlier first‑principles studies.
[claim] Assuming the order‑disorder interface energy is half the anti‑phase boundary energy, the interface energy employed in phase‑field simulations is approximately 15.45 mJ m⁻².
[claim] Monte Carlo‑derived voltage profiles at 300 K match experimental measurements except that the metal‑insulator transition plateau near x≈0.8‑0.9 is not captured because the O3 structure was used.

[method] Matbench Discovery
[claim] EquiformerV2+DeNS (a universal interatomic potential) achieves the highest classification performance among all evaluated models, with F1 scores up to 0.983, ROC AUC 0.96, and discovery acceleration factors up to 6.33, establishing state‑of‑the‑art for ML‑guided materials discovery.
[claim] Training universal interatomic potential models with forces, stresses, and magnetic moments substantially improves stability‑prediction performance compared with energy‑only models, enhancing both classification metrics (F1, DAF) and regression metrics (MAE, RMSE).
[claim] Regression‑based metrics such as MAE, RMSE, and R² are poorly aligned with classification‑based metrics needed for materials‑discovery tasks, and improvements in these regression metrics do not necessarily translate into higher F1 or discovery acceleration scores.
[claim] The WBM test set contains 215,488 unique prototype structures (32,942 thermodynamically stable), is enriched in actinides, lanthanides, metalloids and noble‑transition metals while under‑representing oxygen, is dominated by ternary phases (~75 %), and most structures have fewer than 100 atomic sites, contrasting with the Materials Project training distribution.
[claim] Prospective benchmarking that introduces covariate shift between training and test distributions provides a more realistic indicator of real‑world discovery performance than retrospective split strategies, and requires training and test sets larger than the training set to evaluate model scalability.
[claim] Random‑forest models excel on small datasets but are outperformed by neural‑network models on large datasets due to the benefits of representation learning.
[claim] Optimizing hyperparameters solely for the Matbench Discovery benchmark may degrade performance of models intended for general‑purpose use.
[claim] Models trained on Materials Project data systematically underpredict convex‑hull distances because the training set is biased toward low‑formation‑energy (stable) structures.
[claim] High disagreement among model predictions (large standard deviation) can be used to flag potential DFT relaxation failures in high‑throughput screenings.
[claim] Accurate regression models can still produce high false‑positive rates near the 0 eV/atom convex‑hull decision boundary.
[claim] Using the MACE checkpoint trained on the M3GNet dataset caused volume implosion failures for several hundred of the 250 k test crystals, whereas the checkpoint trained on the MPtrj dataset reduced failures to only 44 crystals.
[claim] Extrapolation performance degrades with increasing WBM batch number for most models, especially Wrenformer and Voronoi RF, while universal interatomic potential models (e.g., EquiformerV2, ORB) show minimal degradation across batches.
