[method] GNoME
[claim] GNoME discovered 2.2 million crystal structures stable with respect to the Materials Project, with 381,000 newly on the convex hull, representing an order-of-magnitude expansion from all previous discoveries.
[claim] 736 GNoME-discovered structures match experimentally validated ICSD structures, with 184 representing novel discoveries since the project began.
[claim] GNoME achieves hit rates above 80% for structural predictions and 33% for composition-only predictions, compared to 1% in previous work, with active learning improving from less than 6% and 3% respectively over six rounds.
[claim] Final GNoME models predict energies with a mean absolute error of 11 meV per atom on relaxed structures, improved from 21 meV per atom in the initial model trained on Materials Project data.
[claim] GNNs trained on large and diverse first-principles calculations increase the number of stable crystals by more than an order of magnitude, with scaling showing consistent power-law improvements in MLIP accuracy and generalization on out-of-distribution structural tasks.
[claim] Large-scale pretraining of MLIPs on GNoME dataset enables models with unprecedented zero-shot accuracy on downstream AIMD data, outperforming state-of-the-art NequIP models trained on hundreds of structures from the target distribution.
[claim] GNoME discovered crystals correspond to 45,500 novel prototypes, a 5.6x increase from the 8,000 in Materials Project.
[claim] GNoME discovers approximately 52,000 layered materials compared to approximately 1,000 in Materials Project, and finds 528 promising Li-ion conductors, a 25x increase compared to the original study.
[claim] GNoME enables efficient discovery of materials with 4+ unique elements, which have been difficult for previous discovery efforts.
[claim] More than 10⁹ candidate structures were generated over the course of active learning using symmetry-aware partial substitutions and random structure search, with 232,477 out of 381,000 stable structures (approximately 61%) attributed to the SAPS candidate generation procedure.
[claim] GNoME-driven molecular dynamics simulations on 623 materials with previously unseen compositions enable classification of unseen compositions as superionic conductors in comparison with AIMD.
[claim] Crystal structures, data, and software for analyzing stable crystals, phase diagrams, static GNN, and interatomic potentials will be made available at the Google DeepMind materials_discovery GitHub repository and via the Materials Project with permanent DOI link 10.17188/2009989.

[method] Gaussian Approximation Potential (GAP) for silicon
[claim] The Gaussian Approximation Potential (GAP) for silicon reproduces density functional theory reference results across a wide range of observable properties, including bulk crystal, liquid, amorphous phases, and point, line, and plane defects.
[claim] For bulk elastic constants (B, C11, C12, C44) the GAP model achieves fractional errors of less than 10% relative to DFT, outperforming all other evaluated interatomic potentials.
[claim] Surface energies of the (111), (110) and (100) silicon cleavage planes are predicted by GAP with errors of around 2% relative to DFT, which is comparable or better than other potentials.
[claim] Formation energies of vacancy and interstitial point defects (hexagonal, tetrahedral, dumbbell) are predicted by GAP within 10% of DFT values, providing uniform accuracy across these defects.
[claim] For extrapolative planar defects not included in the training set—specifically the (112) Σ3 grain boundary and unstable stacking fault energies on the (111) shuffle and glide planes—GAP errors remain within 20% of DFT, outperforming other models.
[claim] Combining a simple repulsive pair potential with a many‑body SOAP‑kernel term in the GAP framework yields meV‑per‑atom accuracy for silicon energetics.
[claim] The Gaussian process regression framework underlying GAP provides an uncertainty quantification that qualitatively estimates the potential’s accuracy for any given atomic configuration.
[claim] Using the GAP model enables simulations that would be prohibitively expensive with DFT, such as finite‑temperature phase‑boundary calculations, liquid self‑diffusivity, amorphous silicon formation by slow quench, and dynamic brittle fracture.
[claim] A training database of manageable size, constructed from DFT configurations covering relevant phases and defects, is sufficient to achieve high transferability of the GAP model across diverse silicon configurations.
[claim] Benchmark comparisons show that the new GAP model yields lower errors than previous GAP models for silicon.
[claim] The Smooth Overlap of Atomic Positions (SOAP) kernel captures the regularity of the silicon potential energy surface, leading to accurate interpolation within the sampled configuration space.

[method] Universal HamGNN Hamiltonian model
[claim] The universal HamGNN model achieves a mean absolute error of 5.4 meV for the real‑space Hamiltonian matrix on the test set after the first round of training.
[claim] Fine‑tuning the universal model on a small MOF dataset reduces the Hamiltonian matrix MAE to approximately 3.95 meV.
[claim] The universal HamGNN model accurately predicts the energy band structures and charge densities of complex multi‑element crystals (e.g., Hf2Zr9Ta6Ti5Nb5B54, HfTaTiB4MoC4, K3Ba3Li2Al4B6O20F), matching DFT results.
[claim] For the disordered solid‑electrolyte Li10Si1.5P1.5S11.5Cl0.5, the universal model predicts an insulating behavior with a band gap of 1.4 eV.
[claim] The universal HamGNN model accurately predicts the electronic structure of low‑dimensional systems, including a 1625‑atom MoS2/WS2 twisted bilayer (3.5°) and a C60 cluster, reproducing DFT band structures and HOMO wavefunctions.
[claim] High‑throughput screening of 188,722 GeNOME crystals with the universal model identifies 21,973 insulators (3,940 direct‑gap) and 5,109 flat‑band materials, nearly doubling the entries in the Materials Flatband Database.
[claim] Using the universal HamGNN model reduces computational cost by several orders of magnitude compared with DFT (e.g., 0.33 core·hours versus 181 core·hours for a large MOF) while preserving accuracy of band gaps and charge‑density differences.
[claim] A two‑step training procedure—first minimizing real‑space Hamiltonian error, then adding orbital‑energy error at random k‑points—is essential to obtain a truly universal Hamiltonian model.
[claim] Incorporating orbital‑energy loss in a second fine‑tuning round markedly improves band‑structure predictions, yielding energy bands and Fermi surfaces that closely match DFT calculations for the test set.
[claim] The universal HamGNN model generalizes to crystals containing more than five distinct elements and to any element supported by the OpenMX PBE pseudopotential library, effectively covering the entire periodic table.

[method] D4FT
[claim] The QR‑based reparameterization used in D4FT preserves the orthonormal constraints of Kohn‑Sham orbitals, making the search space equivalent to the original orthogonal function space, as proved in Proposition 3.1, and can be interpreted as projected gradient descent on the orthogonal constraint set.
[claim] Direct minimization of the total KS‑DFT energy with stochastic gradient descent reduces the asymptotic computational complexity from O(N⁴) to O(N³), and the full‑batch D4FT algorithm has complexity O(nN²)+O(n²N²), which is lower than the O(n²N²) complexity of conventional SCF; minibatch training further lowers the cost.
[claim] D4FT converges to a self‑consistent Kohn‑Sham solution that satisfies the eigenfunction condition.
[claim] Across a benchmark set ranging from He to benzene, D4FT reproduces ground‑state energies of the reference PySCF implementation with deviations ≤0.02 Ha (LSDA/6‑31g and LSDA/STO‑3g).
[claim] D4FT correctly predicts the paramagnetic ground state of O₂ and the diamagnetic ground state of CO₂ by comparing spin‑restricted and spin‑unrestricted calculations.
[claim] D4FT scales to carbon clusters up to C₁₈₀, achieving wall‑clock runtimes an order of magnitude faster (≈1100 s for C₁₈₀) than PySCF, GPAW, Psi4, and JAX‑SCF.
[claim] Incorporating a neural local scaling transformation as a learnable basis (preserving the overlap matrix) enhances wave‑function expressiveness and yields lower LSDA ground‑state energies for atoms (He, Li, Be, C, N, O) compared with the raw STO‑3g basis.
[claim] D4FT converges faster than JAX‑SCF, demonstrating a smaller computational complexity and reduced number of iterations.
[claim] D4FT provides a unified optimization algorithm with a stronger convergence guarantee than traditional SCF fixed‑point iteration.
[claim] D4FT successfully converges on unstable fullerene fragments (C₁₂₀, C₁₄₀) where PySCF fails to converge within the default iteration limit.
[claim] Standard numerical integration based on truncated series expansions may incur large truncation errors for fully neural wave functions, suggesting Monte Carlo integration as a more suitable alternative.
[claim] The stochastic nature of SGD makes D4FT’s convergence sensitive to minibatch size and optimizer choice, with very small batches accelerating epoch convergence but potentially degrading wall‑clock time.

[method] Atomic Cluster Expansion extended to scalar, vectorial, tensorial properties with magnetic moments and charge transfer
[claim] The atomic cluster expansion (ACE) is generalized to model scalar, vectorial and tensorial atomic properties and to include additional atomic degrees of freedom—species, magnetic moments, and charges—on equal footing with atomic positions.
[claim] The derived ACE formulas enable efficient evaluation of forces and magnetic torques.
[claim] At the lowest order, the magnetic ACE reproduces a distance‑dependent Heisenberg interaction.
[claim] Representing tensors with spherical harmonics yields a dramatically sparser basis, where a rank‑N Cartesian tensor with 3^N components can be represented by (N+1)^2 spherical harmonics (e.g., a 10th‑order tensor requires 121 harmonics instead of 59 049 Cartesian components).
[claim] Moments Tensor Potentials (MTP) and the Spectral Neighbor Analysis Potential (SNAP) can be expressed exactly as special cases of the ACE.
[claim] Neglecting spin‑orbit coupling forces all magnetic angular momenta to be zero, greatly reducing the number of ACE expansion coefficients, since the magnetic contribution to the cohesive energy is only about 10 % of the total.
[claim] The ACE formulation is invariant under translation, rotation, inversion and permutation of identical atoms.
[claim] Although the full magnetic and charge‑transfer ACE contains many parameters, hierarchical ordering of interactions allows robust and systematic fitting to reference data.
[claim] Implementing the extended ACE for vectorial, tensorial, magnetic and charge degrees of freedom requires no significantly greater effort than the original scalar ACE implementation.
[claim] Because the ACE basis is complete and hierarchical, it can in principle achieve arbitrary accuracy for any scalar, vectorial or tensorial property.

[claim] The GNN predicts atomic von Mises stress in polycrystalline graphene with a mean normalized relative error of 5.5% and a maximum error below 7% on a test set of 400 crystals.
[claim] The GNN predicts atomic tensile stress in porous graphene membranes under tensile strain with a mean normalized relative error of 4.9% and a maximum error of about 10%.
[claim] The GNN reproduces the linear decrease of Young’s modulus with vacancy concentration in porous graphene, matching MD results and yielding the fitted relation E = 823.7 − 5635.6·Cv (GPa).
[claim] In polycrystalline aluminum, the GNN predicts atomic potential energy with a mean normalized relative error of 11.0% (maximum ≈13%) and achieves R² = 0.99 for mean potential energy versus grain number.
[claim] Including tensile strain as an input node feature enables the GNN to accurately predict stress evolution during loading, reproducing nonlinear strain‑stress curves for porous graphene.
[claim] The GNN’s stress predictions are substantially more accurate than on‑the‑fly stress calculations from the force field, which exhibit higher errors.
[claim] The GNN framework generalizes across defect types (grain boundaries, vacancies) and material dimensionalities (2D graphene, 3D aluminum), and to unseen defect configurations in over 10⁶ porous graphene structures, maintaining high prediction accuracy despite being trained on only about 1,200 random samples.
[claim] Coupling the GNN with a genetic algorithm efficiently discovers optimal holey graphene designs (e.g., arrow‑shaped hole patterns) that achieve significantly lower stress concentration than suboptimal designs, using only ~800 stress evaluations—an order of magnitude fewer than brute‑force search—and reliably locates the global minimum in most of 1,000 random initializations.
[claim] The GNN respects physical constraints, accurately capturing derivative properties such as stress fields that obey underlying physical laws, and predicts global properties (Young’s modulus, total potential energy) that follow known physical relationships and match MD results across different crystalline systems.
[claim] The Principal Neighbourhood Aggregation (PNA) GNN model achieves the lowest mean and variance of test mean‑squared error among GCN, GAT, and MPNN (sum and max) variants on the polycrystalline graphene dataset.
[claim] The GNN accelerates atomic property prediction by hundreds to thousands of times compared with conventional MD simulations, requiring seconds on a single CPU versus thousands of seconds on 24 CPUs.
[claim] Linear fitting of atomic properties yields substantially higher prediction errors than the GNN approach, demonstrating the superiority of the nonlinear GNN model for mapping initial structures to final property distributions.

[method] LiFlow
[claim] LiFlow predicts lithium mean‑squared displacement with a Spearman rank correlation of 0.7–0.8 on unseen material compositions, enabling screening of high‑diffusivity electrolytes.
[claim] LiFlow achieves speed‑ups of up to ~600,000× over ab initio molecular dynamics (and ~400× over MLIP), predicting a 1 ns trajectory in 48 s for a 2 × 2 × 1 LGPS supercell and 352 s for a 4 × 4 × 4 supercell.
[claim] The computational cost of LiFlow scales linearly with the number of atoms (O(n)), in contrast to the cubic scaling (O(n³)) of ab initio molecular dynamics.
[claim] Incorporating an adaptive, thermally and chemically conditioned Maxwell–Boltzmann prior markedly lowers mean absolute errors and raises rank correlations for MSD and RDF compared with an isotropic prior; ablation studies show performance degradation without it.
[claim] Incorporating the Corrector model reduces RDF mean absolute error and mitigates large‑displacement artifacts, improving MSD prediction across temperatures, especially for hydrogen diffusion.
[claim] LiFlow trained on 25 ps ab initio molecular dynamics trajectories can generate stable trajectories up to 1 ns in larger (4 × 4 × 4) supercells, reproducing lithium self‑diffusivity, activation energies, and temperature dependence comparable to long AIMD simulations.
[claim] Within the training temperature range, LiFlow’s predicted diffusivity D* closely matches reference values from Winter and Gómez‑Bombarelli.
[claim] A direct regression (Regressor) model yields higher mean‑squared‑displacement errors than the generative LiFlow model, demonstrating the necessity of generative modeling for accurate atomic transport simulation.
[claim] When extrapolating to temperatures lower than the training range, LiFlow’s predicted diffusivity D* decreases more slowly than reference data, indicating fictitious diffusive behavior at high 1000/T.
[claim] The adaptive prior classifier provides limited benefit at the lowest temperature (600 K), reducing its overall effectiveness under that condition.
[claim] LiFlow qualitatively captures ion transport behavior in sodium‑based conductors despite being trained only on lithium‑containing materials.
[claim] LiFlow reproduces structural features such as diffusion traces, probability densities, and potentials of mean force for lithium; accuracy is high at lower temperatures with only slight deviations at higher temperatures.

[method] AFLOW high-throughput materials discovery framework
[claim] AFLOW can automatically calculate a wide suite of physical observables across a large database of structures with minimal human intervention.
[claim] AFLOW detects most calculation failures, automatically corrects input parameters, restarts calculations, and can run as a Unix daemon to generate, run, correct, and converge many DFT jobs per day, yielding higher throughput than manual management.
[claim] AFLOW provides a standardized definition of Brillouin‑zone integration paths for all 14 Bravais lattices, filling a gap in the literature.
[claim] AFLOW reproduces experimental phonon dispersion curves for face‑centered cubic Rhodium, showing excellent agreement with measured data.
[claim] AFLOW’s cage‑finding algorithm identifies interstitial sites via a topological method, finding 14 cages (6 octahedral, 8 tetrahedral) that reduce to 5 symmetrically inequivalent positions, with radii of 2.2225 Å (octahedral) and 1.9248 Å (tetrahedral).
[claim] AFLOW can automatically generate high‑index surface slabs for complex multicomponent compounds, demonstrated for (001), (110) and (111) slabs of an fcc L10 binary.
[claim] AFLOW can automatically create nanoparticle structures of arbitrary radius and separation, enabling high‑throughput nanoparticle studies.
[claim] AFLOW can automatically construct convex hulls for binary alloy systems at zero temperature using formation enthalpies from DFT calculations.
[claim] The AFLOW database currently contains approximately 400 experimental prototype structures and several million bcc/fcc/hcp‑derived superstructures.
[claim] A hybrid HSE06 calculation for ZnO yields a band gap of 2.48 eV, substantially larger than the LDA/GGA gap of 0.7 eV and the PBE+U gap of 1.82 eV.
[claim] Tuning the exact‑exchange fraction α to 0.375 in HSE06 brings the calculated ZnO band gap into agreement with experiment.
[claim] Hybrid functional calculations scale approximately as O(N^2.5) for small systems and linearly beyond ~15 Å (HSE06) or ~100 Å (PBE0), whereas standard GGA calculations scale as O(N^3).

[method] OMat24 dataset
[claim] OMat24 comprises over 118 million DFT calculations across diverse chemistries, materials, and configurations for inorganic bulk materials, making it up to 2 orders of magnitude larger than other openly available datasets in terms of number of single-point calculations.
[claim] OMat24 exhibits more uniform and comprehensive coverage of near-neighbor pairs and element distributions compared to both Alexandria and MPtrj datasets, with elemental coverage spanning most of the periodic table.
[claim] OMat24 contains a large fraction of far-from-equilibrium structures with 1 to 100 atoms per structure (majority having less than 20 atoms), yielding broader label distributions than relaxation-only datasets.
[claim] MLIP models trained on OMat24 achieve F1 scores above 0.9 for stability prediction and 20 meV/atom accuracy for formation energy on Matbench Discovery, with all five top-performing models on the Matbench Discovery leaderboard exclusively trained on OMat24.
[claim] The eSEN model achieves an F1 score of 0.925 and energy-above-hull MAE of 18 meV/atom when pretrained on OMat24, with eSEN and equiformerV2 models with DeNS outperforming their non-DeNS counterparts and all other third-party models in the Matbench Discovery benchmark task.
[claim] OMat24's diversity corrects the systematic softening bias of prior models trained on less diverse datasets, with systematic softening improvements across all degrees consistently observed in five distinct architectures, indicating the effect is largely architecture-independent.
[claim] Training on OMat24 results in models with better extrapolation to regions with lower dataset density farther away from the convex hull compared to models trained on other datasets.
[claim] The mean absolute difference in formation energies between MP and OMat24 DFT settings is 13.5 meV/atom across 423 compounds, with differences largely attributed to different versions of pseudo-potentials and different pseudo-potential symbols for Yb and W.
[claim] The mean absolute error between DFT predicted and experimental formation energies for 222 compounds is 55 meV/atom using OMat24 DFT settings, with compatibility corrections computed following the Materials Project MP2020 Compatibility scheme.
[claim] Machine-learned interatomic potentials trained on OMat24 predict tightly converged DFT forces with accuracy comparable to or better than predictions for less tightly converged calculations.
[claim] A two-step training strategy with direct force pretraining followed by conservative finetuning results in eSEN models with higher accuracy requiring less total training epochs and time compared to training conservative models from scratch.
[claim] The diversity of the larger OMat24 dataset does not benefit from the regularization or augmentation provided by DeNS, whereas dataset augmentation techniques like DeNS can significantly enhance performance when training solely on the MPtraj dataset.

[method] Automatminer
[claim] Matbench v0.1 is a benchmark suite containing 13 supervised machine learning tasks (10 regression, 3 classification) for materials property prediction, with dataset sizes ranging from 312 to 132,752 samples.
[claim] Matbench contains data from 10 density functional theory-derived and experimental sources including Materials Project, Zhuo et al., Landolt-Bornstein Handbook, Castelli et al., JARVIS DFT 2D, and Citrine Informatics.
[claim] Matbench tasks include predicting optical, thermal, electronic, thermodynamic, tensile, and elastic properties given materials composition and/or crystal structure.
[claim] Automatminer is a fully-automated machine learning pipeline consisting of four stages (autofeaturization, cleaning, dimensionality reduction, and AutoML search) that requires no user intervention or hyperparameter tuning.
[claim] Automatminer Express preset achieves the best performance on 8 of 13 tasks in the Matbench benchmark.
[claim] Automatminer's auto-generated models outperform or equal the Random Forest model across all Matbench tasks except predicting formation energies across the Materials Project.
[claim] Graph network models (CGCNN and MEGNet) have high errors on small datasets (<10^4 samples) but leverage large datasets more efficiently, outperforming traditional ML and AutoML approaches on tasks with approximately 10^4 data points or more.
[claim] Descriptor-based Automatminer and RF models have lower errors on small datasets but their improvement rates are shallower, with AutoML's advantage over conventional techniques narrowing as sample count increases and essentially lost near 10^5 samples.
[claim] All algorithms exhibit a universal trend of decreasing relative errors as dataset size increases.
[claim] For small datasets (<10^4 samples), inexpensive Automatminer presets (~1-5 minute training) retain the bulk of performance compared to expensive presets (24h+ training), with Express retaining 95% or more of the accuracy of more expensive presets at less than 50% of the computational cost on data-scarce tasks.
[claim] Graph networks (CGCNN and MEGNet) far outperform traditional ML algorithms on formation energy prediction tasks, with MEGNet decisively outperforming Automatminer for the PhDOS task; among nine structure-based tasks, Automatminer and MEGNet each achieve best scores on 4 tasks.
[claim] Matbench provides a consistent evaluation framework using five-fold nested cross-validation on identical folds across all algorithms to minimize comparison bias, with datasets pre-cleaned to remove unphysical computed data and task-irrelevant experimental data.

[method] MLIP-NEB benchmarking workflow
[claim] MACE-MP-0 achieves the lowest mean absolute error (0.310 eV) in migration barrier predictions across the entire Dataset-2 of 574 migration paths.
[claim] Orb-v3 achieves the lowest MAE (0.198 eV) when evaluated on non-outlier data points (excluding systems with absolute errors >1 eV).
[claim] Orb-v3 and SevenNet classify materials as good versus bad ionic conductors with accuracy greater than 82% using a 500 meV migration barrier threshold.
[claim] All MLIPs struggle with high migration barrier predictions, with only 3.7-20.7% achieving acceptable accuracy (<0.1 eV error) in the 1.31-2.50 eV range.
[claim] There is no evident correlation between migration barrier prediction accuracy and local geometry prediction accuracy across all MLIPs.
[claim] SevenNet exhibits the highest fraction of good local geometry predictions (0.719) while MACE-MP-0 exhibits the lowest fraction of bad geometry predictions (0.190) among all tested MLIPs.
[claim] MACE-MP-0 and SevenNet intermediate images provide better initial guesses relative to conventional interpolation techniques in over 71% of structures.
[claim] MLIP-NEB relaxations produce intermediate image geometries closer to DFT-NEB references than linear interpolation in over 66% of structures.
[claim] M3GNet and CHGNet exhibit systematic bias toward underestimating migration barriers, with 73.1% and 78.2% of predictions being underestimates respectively.
[claim] For high migration barrier systems, MLIPs achieve their best geometry predictions but worst barrier predictions, indicating an inverse relationship.
[claim] CHGNet and M3GNet demonstrate superior performance for materials with low migration barriers but lack consistency over wider barrier ranges.
[claim] Orb-v3 exhibits the slowest degradation in prediction accuracy as migration barrier values increase compared to other MLIPs.

[method] Orb-v3
[claim] Orb-v3 achieves near state-of-the-art performance across evaluations with at least 10x reduction in latency and 8x reduction in memory compared to alternative MLIPs.
[claim] Orb-v3-direct-20 uses only 32.8GB GPU memory for 100,000 atom systems and completes in under half a second, while all baseline methods and conservative models encounter Out Of Memory errors.
[claim] Orb-v3-direct-* models are the only universal MLIPs that can compute hundreds of forward passes per second, exceeding one million steps per hour for small systems.
[claim] Orb-v3-conservative-inf-omat achieves the highest accuracy for almost all physical property metrics while being faster than any best-performing model currently available in literature.
[claim] Orb-v3-direct-20-omat is comparable in accuracy to current state-of-the-art models while being approximately 30 times faster than SevenNet.
[claim] Only orb-v3-conservative-inf is truly energy-conserving in NVE molecular dynamics simulations; all other Orb-v3 variants exhibit energy drift.
[claim] Orb-v3 can simulate the carbonic anhydrase II enzyme system with over 20,000 atoms under fully solvated conditions for over 700 ps without unphysical behavior.
[claim] Orb-v3 models achieve competitive thermal conductivity prediction (κSRME), demonstrating direct models can yield smooth second- and third-order derivatives of the potential energy surface.
[claim] Non-equivariant, non-conservative architectures can accurately model physical properties including those requiring higher-order derivatives of the potential energy surface.
[claim] Equigrad regularization improves rotational invariance of Orb-v3 by approximately 5x compared to default loss training.
[claim] The intrinsic confidence head predictions from Orb-v3 correlate well with atomic force MAE at the atom level, even for out-of-distribution datasets.
[claim] Neighbor limits induce discontinuities in the potential energy surface that create performance penalties for certain calculations.

[method] Virtual Node Graph Neural Network
[claim] Virtual Node Graph Neural Network (VGNN) enables graph neural networks to handle variable output dimensions by incorporating virtual nodes that resemble phonon dynamical matrices.
[claim] Three virtual node approaches were developed: vector virtual nodes (VVN) outputting 3m Γ-phonon branches, matrix virtual nodes (MVN) with m² 3×3 matrices, and momentum-dependent matrix virtual nodes (k-MVN) for full band structure prediction.
[claim] VGNN achieves direct prediction of Γ-phonon spectra and full phonon dispersion using only atomic coordinates as input without prior knowledge of interatomic forces.
[claim] VGNN-based phonon calculation achieves significantly faster computation speed than ab initio methods (DFPT, frozen-phonon) while maintaining reasonable accuracy.
[claim] Computing Γ-phonon spectra for 146,323 Materials Project materials took less than five hours on an eight-GPU system, even for materials with over 400 atoms per unit cell.
[claim] MVN outperforms VVN for Γ-phonon prediction, especially for complex materials, at the cost of slightly higher computational expense.
[claim] The k-MVN method can predict full phonon band structures at arbitrary k points in the Brillouin zone by incorporating momentum dependence through phase factors for unit-cell translations.
[claim] The approach generalizes to materials with varying atom counts, tested on systems with 2–40 atoms (training) and over 40 atoms (testing).
[claim] The k-MVN model can handle phonon prediction for alloys ranging from binary to five-component high entropy alloys by encoding atomic composition through weighted atomic masses.
[claim] A Γ-phonon database containing phonon spectra for 146,323 Materials Project materials was generated using the MVN approach, with unit cell atom counts ranging from 1 to 444 atoms.
[claim] The model was trained on a DFPT computational database containing phonon dispersion data for 1,521 crystalline inorganic materials.
[claim] For very complicated materials, VVN-predicted phonons tend to have higher frequencies than ground truth, and prediction loss becomes larger as input materials become more complicated.

[method] DeePMD-kit v2
[claim] DeePMD-kit is an open-source software package that facilitates molecular dynamics simulations using Deep Potential machine learning potentials for computational chemistry and materials science.
[claim] DeePMD-kit supports multiple atomic descriptor types including local frame, DeepPot-SE, attention-based, and hybrid descriptors.
[claim] The DeepPot-SE descriptor is continuous up to the second-order derivative in its domain, unlike the local frame descriptor which is not smooth at the cutoff radius and when exchanging the order of two nearest neighbors.
[claim] None of the tested descriptors outperforms the others in terms of accuracy across all datasets.
[claim] Type embedding reduces the number of neural network parameters and improves computing efficiency for systems with large numbers of chemical species by having all species share the same network parameters.
[claim] Compressed models are 1x-10x faster than the original models for both training and inference.
[claim] NVNMD (non-von Neumann molecular dynamics) is 50x-100x faster than regular MD simulations.
[claim] FP32 precision is 0.5x to 2x faster than FP64 precision in nearly all tested systems while demonstrating similar validation errors.
[claim] The DPLR model adds electrostatic energy to the total energy, with electrostatic energy calculated in Fourier space for modeling long-range interactions.
[claim] The fitting network can fit potential energy, force, virial, and tensorial properties such as dipole and polarizability.
[claim] Model deviation is defined as the standard deviation of properties inferred by an ensemble of models trained with independently initialized parameters.
[claim] DeePMD-kit APIs have been integrated into multiple third-party MD packages including LAMMPS, i-PI, GROMACS, AMBER, OpenMM, and ABACUS.

[method] ml_multiscale_modeling_perspective
[claim] Machine learning can serve as a surrogate for, accelerate, or augment traditional numerical methods in multiscale computational modeling.
[claim] ML-based simulation can achieve comparable fidelity to direct numerical simulation while being considerably faster in computation time, with convolutional neural networks producing high-fidelity estimation of materials microstructure response with multiple orders of magnitude faster computation.
[claim] Hierarchical multiscale modeling approaches require large amounts of memory and storage space to store precomputed quantities of interest.
[claim] Concurrent multiscale modeling approaches face formidable computation costs as the problem size increases.
[claim] Trained ML models are typically only effective for interpolating data points and may not be reliable when extrapolating beyond the known data range.
[claim] Most common ML techniques such as CNNs are limited to specific discretization settings and do not generalize well to settings that differ from training data discretization.
[claim] Neural operators can make predictions that are not affected by discretization settings while maintaining prediction accuracy.
[claim] Physics-informed machine learning and transfer learning can reduce the need for large datasets while maintaining prediction accuracy and performance of ML models.
[claim] Physics-naïve ML architectures often fail to capture underlying physical laws despite having relatively high prediction performance.
[claim] Meta-learning allows ML algorithms to quickly learn and adapt to new tasks by leveraging experience from solving similar tasks with relatively small datasets.
[claim] ML can accelerate the solution of inverse problems by providing direct design solutions without requiring traditional iterative optimization processes.
[claim] Koopman operator theory allows highly nonlinear dynamical systems to be represented in terms of an infinite-dimensional linear operator.

[method] AFLOW high-throughput DFT calculation protocol
[claim] The AFLOW standard enables reproducible high-throughput DFT calculations through standardized parameter sets for k-point density, energy cut-offs, exchange-correlation functionals, pseudopotentials, DFT+U parameters, and convergence criteria.
[claim] The AFLOWLIB repository contains calculated properties of over 625,000 materials across Binary Alloy Project, Electronic Structure database, Heusler database, and Elements database.
[claim] AFLOW calculations follow a standardized sequential workflow: RELAX1 → RELAX2 → STATIC → BANDS for materials in the Elements, ICSD, and Heusler databases.
[claim] Default NKPPRA values for non-BANDS calculations vary by database: Binary Alloy uses 6000 for RELAX, Heusler uses 10000 for STATIC and 6000 for RELAX, and ICSD uses 10000 for STATIC and 8000 for RELAX.
[claim] The PBE functional combined with PAW potentials is the default exchange-correlation functional and potential combination for ICSD, Binary Alloy, and Heusler databases.
[claim] The applied plane-wave kinetic energy cut-off (Ecut) is the largest recommended value among all species in the calculation, increased by a factor of 1.4.
[claim] DFT+U corrections are applied to the entire ICSD database and certain Heusler database entries containing O, S, Se, and F elements, but not to the Binary Alloy database.
[claim] Specific Ueff parameters are defined for d-block elements (Table 4) and U, J parameters for f-block elements (Table 5) to correct self-interaction error in DFT+U calculations, with values ranging from 1.9 eV (In) to 7.5 eV (Zn).
[claim] The first RELAX calculation is performed in collinear spin-polarized fashion with initial magnetic moments set to 1.0 µB per atom, and spin polarization is turned off in subsequent calculations if magnetization is below 0.025 µB/atom.
[claim] Electronic convergence criteria are δEelec = 10⁻⁵ eV and ionic convergence criteria are δEion = 10⁻⁴ eV for Elements database entries, while all other databases use δEelec = 10⁻³ eV and δEion = 10⁻² eV.
[claim] Following the AFLOW standard enables materials science researchers to reproduce AFLOWLIB consortium results and make direct comparisons of properties between different materials for identifying trends and formulating design rules.
[claim] BANDS calculations use 128 k-points per segment for single element structures and 20 k-points for compounds along high-symmetry paths.

[method] DeePMD training protocol for diffusion coefficient computation
[claim] The DeePMD model successfully reproduces the superionic behavior of solid-state electrolytes with linear Lithium/Sodium mean squared displacement over time and diffusion coefficient uncertainty of about 20% or smaller, which is precise enough for battery applications.
[claim] The DeePMD model provides excellent energy conservation in all tested systems up to 2 ns of NVE dynamics.
[claim] For LLZO, the computed activation energies range from 0.2 to 0.22 eV, in very good agreement with experimental values of 0.20-0.21 eV for cubic LLZO.
[claim] For LGPS, the computed activation energy is 0.16 eV, which is slightly lower than experimental values (0.22 eV) but in line with previous computational studies (0.17-0.21 eV).
[claim] For NASICON, training starting from PFF-MD configurations with 480 atoms achieves convergence during the first training loop with activation energy around 0.2 eV.
[claim] For NASICON, training starting from FPMD configurations with 80 atoms fails to converge even after three training loops with activation energies spanning 0.2-0.4 eV.
[claim] Starting the training loop with PFF-MD configurations leads to faster convergence than starting with short FPMD trajectories because larger simulation cells can be used.
[claim] Training set cleaning procedures including minimum ion-ion distance cutoff, energy/force outlier removal, and loss condition monitoring are necessary to help the algorithm converge to a physical model.
[claim] The proposed training protocol based on augmenting the training set via intermediate molecular dynamics simulations can assess the quality of approximate trajectories and computed physical properties.
[claim] Starting the training loop with sufficient data sampling a relevant portion of phase space is important for obtaining generalizable models.
[claim] The DeePMD model is a promising candidate for developing a universal potential for solid-state electrolytes, though care must be taken when selecting training configurations.
[claim] For LLZO, results are quite insensitive to the choice of cell volume (NPT equilibrated vs experimental cif-file values) for producing the initial training set.

[claim] FastCHGNet trains in 1.5 hours using 32 GPUs compared to 8.3 days on a single A100 GPU for the original CHGNet model.
[claim] MLIPs map atomic configurations to total energy and provide forces and stresses as analytical derivatives of the potential energy surface.
[claim] MLIPs use highly flexible functional forms (e.g., neural networks) while PBPs use highly constrained forms guided by physical intuition (e.g., Lennard-Jones).
[claim] Approximately 40% of the UK's academic HPC was spent on DFT calculations in a recent year, most of which was AIMD.
[claim] EquiformerV2-OMAT24 achieves the best performance on the MatBench leaderboard as of this writing.
[claim] Each cataloged DFT structure provides one energy and 3N forces (N = number of atoms) for training universal MLIPs.
[claim] Pre-trained targeted MLIPs for specific systems can be found on the NIST Interatomic Potentials Repository and OpenKIM.
[claim] CHGNet achieves test mean absolute errors of 29 meV/atom for energy, 70 meV/Angstrom for force, and 0.308 GPa for stress.
[claim] M3GNet achieves test mean absolute errors of 35 meV/atom for energy, 72 meV/Angstrom for force, and 0.41 GPa for stress.
[claim] CHGNet uniquely includes electronic effects of valences by explicitly embedding magnetic moments on the vector representation of each atom, enabling charge-informed atomistic simulations.
[claim] CHGNet achieved the lowest formation energy MAE at 81 meV/atom, while all other models had MAEs of 129 meV/atom or higher.
[claim] MACE-MP0 performed best for discovering new stable materials with classification F1 score of 0.67, followed by CHGNet (0.61) and M3GNet (0.57).

[method] long-range MLIP generalization framework with biased train-test splitting
[claim] Long-range correction schemes in machine learning interatomic potentials are essential for achieving state-of-the-art accuracy, improving in-distribution performance, and enabling significant gains in transferability to unseen regions of chemical space.
[claim] Latent Ewald Summation cannot infer correct partial charges without reference charge labels and frequently predicts charges near zero or opposite in sign to reference values in challenging chemical environments such as MOFs.
[claim] CELLI-based models trained with reference charges consistently produce physically meaningful results and exhibit good performance across biased split benchmarks on MOF datasets.
[claim] Baseline versions of MACE and Allegro are degenerate with respect to total charge and cannot distinguish between molecules with different charge states without long-range corrections.
[claim] Biased train-test splitting strategies including cluster, maximal separation, size, and random splits enable rigorous benchmarking by explicitly testing model performance in significantly different regions of chemical space.
[claim] EFA enables modeling of long-range interactions without requiring explicit neighbor cutoffs and outperforms CELLI on most benchmarking subsplits when reference charges are unavailable.
[claim] MACE without long-range correction does not generalize well to out-of-distribution samples, while integration of long-range correction schemes has significant effects on both MACE and Allegro architectures.
[claim] Strictly local MLIP models overestimate short-range interactions to compensate for missing or incorrectly modeled long-range contributions.
[claim] Metal-organic frameworks present an ideal application for MLIPs because classical force fields lack required accuracy while DFT is too computationally expensive for large unit cells and long timescales.
[claim] Increasing the number of message passing steps can lead to overfitting and decreased performance compared to baseline models.
[claim] Total charge embeddings can recover much of CELLI's performance on some datasets but generalize poorly in size-based extrapolation and should be viewed as a potential extension rather than replacement for long-range methods.
[claim] The observed improvements from long-range corrections cannot be attributed to increased model capacity as all variants share identical hyperparameters and nearly identical parameter counts.

[method] unconstrained MLIP evaluation framework
[claim] Unconstrained machine-learned interatomic potentials (MLIPs) trained on large datasets achieve accuracies on par with state-of-the-art equivariant architectures while maintaining orders-of-magnitude lower computational cost than quantum-mechanical methods.
[claim] The PET model achieves state-of-the-art accuracy on matbench-discovery benchmark (DAF=6.075, Accuracy=0.977, F1=0.924) and exceeds SOTA on SPICE molecular benchmark across most subsets for both energy and force predictions.
[claim] PET-OMAD demonstrates the best overall accuracy in predicting energies and forces on MADBench in almost all cases, with the highest success rate (98.43%) in predicting desorption reactions.
[claim] Fine-tuning models pre-trained on OMat24 to the MAD dataset achieves near-converged validation metrics in 30-100 epochs versus 700+ epochs when training from scratch, halving validation energy and force errors and achieving 50% lower test error than training on MAD alone.
[claim] Non-conservative (unconstrained) MLIP models consistently show 2-3× theoretical speed-up over their conservative counterparts, with direct force prediction providing additional 2-3× speedup compared to forces computed via automatic differentiation.
[claim] The PET architecture scales to 730M parameters (OMat-XL) while maintaining tractable memory usage and computational efficiency due to increased node representation size and unconstrained architecture.
[claim] Conservative PET-OAM models achieve state-of-the-art performance on phonon tasks in matbench-discovery and the best overall accuracy in predicting shear modulus among tested models.
[claim] Non-conservative models allow residual asymmetries to drive relaxation toward more stable close-packed structures, unlike equivariant models that remain trapped in symmetric but unstable configurations, though 70% (16%) of final configurations retain symmetry of initial structure with 0.01 Å threshold for conservative (non-conservative) models.
[claim] Elastic moduli predictions are very sensitive to the lack of energy conservation in MLIP models, and non-conservative models consistently perform worse on matbench-discovery downstream tasks despite achieving better training and validation accuracies.
[claim] Central finite differences can more than halve the error for non-equivariant models on phonon calculations by averaging out inconsistencies between symmetry-equivalent displacements, and O(3)-averaging increases symmetric structures to 77% with symprec 0.01 Å in the non-conservative case.
[claim] Accurate conservative, rotationally unconstrained models can be used safely for phonon calculations, though it is recommended to use looser convergence tolerances or enforce rotational averaging when performing free geometry optimizations with unconstrained models, especially with direct-force predictions.
[claim] DFT setting inconsistency between training and evaluation datasets significantly affects MLIP model performance comparisons, with PET-OMAD performing worse than PET-OAM and PET-MPtrj on Inorganic Materials due to differences in ab initio theory levels.

[method] two-step supervised-unsupervised melting temperature prediction with symbolic regression
[claim] A curated dataset of 476 binary ionic compound melting temperatures spanning 0-4,000°C was compiled for machine learning model development.
[claim] The best one-step gradient-boosted tree regression model achieves 165±4 K MAE and 0.89 R² on the test set for melting temperature prediction.
[claim] A two-step approach combining unsupervised clustering with supervised regression achieves 156±4 K MAE and 0.92 R², outperforming direct one-step supervised learning.
[claim] Cluster 1 (198 compounds, mostly ionic halides and oxides) achieves 136±5 K MAE and 0.92 R², while Cluster 2 (222 compounds, mostly covalent carbides and nitrides) achieves 189±7 K MAE and 0.90 R².
[claim] Cohesive energy and elastic moduli (shear and bulk modulus) are the most important features for melting temperature prediction, as identified by both ensemble feature importance and SHAP analysis.
[claim] Models trained without elastic moduli features yield errors greater than 400 K, demonstrating that elastic features are necessary for accurate melting temperature predictions.
[claim] Very-high melting temperatures (>3150 K) appear only in Cluster 2, predominantly in metal carbides, reflecting the covalent bonding character of these materials.
[claim] Tree ensemble methods (gradient-boosted trees and random forest regression) substantially outperform linear models, which achieve MAE >240 K and RMSE >340 K, at least 100 K worse than non-linear approaches.
[claim] The two-step clustering approach provides interpretability by revealing different melting physics dominated by bonding types, with Cluster 1 governed by ionic bonding features and Cluster 2 by covalent bonding features.
[claim] VS-SISSO symbolic regression generates interpretable expressions for melting temperature that provide qualitative insight into the melting physics dominating within each cluster.
[claim] Cluster 2 melting temperatures can be accurately represented with symbolic models depending on only two features: squared cohesive energy and inverse square root of periodic groups or electronegativities.
[claim] Symbolic regression results corroborate that cohesive energy and elastic moduli are the most important features, consistent with feature importance and SHAP analysis from tree ensemble models.
